methods.name: M1. Fit one apparition at a time with the period fixed; amplitude = peak-to-peak of the fitted Fourier model, or of phase-binned means
methods.data_type: Sparse or semi-dense survey photometry, one opposition (or one TESS sector) at a time. PTF: at least 20 detections per opposition. iPTF 2015: about 20-min cadence over 4 nights. iPTF 2016: about 10-min cadence over 2-3 nights (corrected; the draft said 10-20 min over 4 nights). TESS: about 27 d of continuous coverage at alpha of roughly 3-8 deg.

methods.algorithm:
Waszczak et al. 2015 (PTF).
- Model (Eq. 1): $V = H + \delta + 5\log_{10}(r\Delta) - 2.5\log_{10}[\phi(\alpha)]$.
- Rotation term (Eq. 6): $\delta \equiv \sum_{k=1,2} A_{1,k}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi k\tau}{P}\right) + A_{2,k}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k\tau}{P}\right)$, with $\tau \equiv t - \Delta/c$.
- The rotation term is fitted together with one of three phase functions: Shevchenko (1997), H-G, or H-G12.
- Periodicity (Eq. 2), $\delta(\tau)=\delta(\tau+nP)$, holds only for $|n| \ll P_{orb}/P$ (Eq. 3), where the synodic orbital period is $P_{orb} = \left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{yr}} - \frac{1}{T_{orb}}\right)^{-1}$ (Eq. 4).
- When the viewing geometry changes, Eq. 2 becomes $\delta(\tau)=F(\tau)\delta(\tau+nP)$ (Eq. 5), where $F(t)=F(t+mT_{orb})$ is an unknown periodic function. For this reason each fit uses data from one opposition only: a 1.1-1.6 yr window centred on the date of minimum alpha, with at least 20 detections.
- Error bars are inflated by a 'cosmic error' that starts at 0.002 mag and is multiplied by 1.5 per iteration until chi2/dof < 3. The fit is aborted if the cosmic error exceeds 0.1 mag.
- The paper says this inflation also makes up for truncating the series at two harmonics. For light curves with narrow eclipse-like dips (their eclipsing-binary example), it inflates the uncertainties and leaves the fitted amplitude underestimated.
- Amplitude definition (Table 2, paraphrased): the fitted amplitude of the folded light curve, equal to the max-min height of the larger of the two peaks.
- Double-peak test, run only when the fitted amplitude is at least 0.1 mag: the ratio of the two peaks must exceed 0.2. The half-frequency solution is chosen if $\chi^2_{min,harmonic} < \chi^2_{min,global} + \text{inv-}\chi^2\text{-cdf}(0.95,7)$.

Chang et al. 2015 and 2016 (iPTF).
- Magnitudes are light-travel-time corrected, reduced to r = Delta = 1 AU, and H uses a fixed G_R = 0.15.
- Fit (Eq. 1): $M_{i,j} = \sum_{k=1,2}^{N_k} B_k\sin\left[\frac{2\pi k}{P}(t_j-t_0)\right] + C_k\cos\left[\frac{2\pi k}{P}(t_j-t_0)\right] + Z_i$, where $Z_i$ is a zero point for each night, field, filter and chip.
- Amplitude: peak-to-peak after discarding the top and bottom 5% of data points.

Pal et al. 2020 (TESS).
- Period search with Eq. 1: $m(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{2}k_i[\alpha(t)-\alpha_0]^i + A\cos[2\pi f(t-T_0)] + B\sin[2\pi f(t-T_0)]$.
- Light curves are folded and binned after the phase-angle correction, at the dominant period and at twice that period.
- The metadata store a peak-to-peak amplitude.

Szabo et al. 2022 (TSSYS-DR1).
- Only light curves meeting the Warner & Harris (2011) 'dense' criterion are used: 8 non-clustered points per night, 8 nights, at most 30 d span.
- Peak-to-peak amplitude is the brightness difference between the brightest and faintest phase bins. The authors chose this because Fourier fits do not always capture the full amplitude of diverse light-curve shapes.

Vavilov & Carry 2025 (TESS).
- Model (Eq. 4): $g(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{k} A_j\cos(2\pi f j t) + B_j\sin(2\pi f j t)$, with k from 1 to 10.
- Phase term $\phi(\alpha)=c_0+c_1\alpha+c_2\alpha^2$ (after Pal 2020), with c1 and c2 bounded by H,G curves.
- Order selection (corrected): pairwise F-tests between all orders; they take the smallest k for which no other order is significantly better at the 95% level. If the chosen fit has only one local maximum, the period is doubled. This is a period-doubling rule, not a filter.
- They show that a 2nd-order series is often insufficient, e.g. for (511) Davida.
- I found no explicit amplitude definition in the text; amplitudes appear only in their plots.

McNeill et al. 2023 (TESS).
- Amplitude comes from a simple sine fitted at the derived period, with G = 0.15 fixed for the phase correction.
- They judged a running mean too crude and found that higher-order Fourier fits gave no clear gain.
methods.assumptions:
- Viewing geometry (aspect and phase angle) is effectively constant within the fitted window: one opposition, or one 27-d sector.
- Principal-axis rotation.
- The phase function removes the mean brightness trend with alpha.
- Waszczak assumes a light curve dominated by the 2nd harmonic, as for an ellipsoid (citing Harris et al. 2014). Vavilov & Carry show that higher orders are often needed.
- No aspect correction is made. Szabo 2022 notes (paraphrased) that a single light curve cannot be corrected for aspect, so its amplitude is only a lower estimate of the a/b asphericity.
methods.validation_reported:
Pal 2020 (only quantitative amplitude-vs-LCDB comparison in this group).
- Compared against the LCDB August 2019 release, which predates the addition of TESS results: 4842 LCDB objects have both a valid period and an amplitude.
- 624 objects overlap with strong enough quality. About 80% have the same period, and about 8% are at double or half the period.
- The Fig. 5 histogram of $A_{LCDB}/A_{TESS}$ has a median of about 1.076.
- The authors attribute the excess to TESS observing near opposition at small phase angles, whereas the LCDB covers many phase angles; they cite Zappala et al. (1990) for the expectation that amplitude grows with phase angle.
- They call the comparison tentative because TESS gives a single epoch and geometry. Vavilov & Carry report TESS alpha typically from 3 to about 8 deg.

Waszczak 2015.
- Validated periods only, using 927 light curves of 805 asteroids with LCDB U = 3. About 1/3 fall in the disagreeing mode (worse than about 3%).
- Fitted amplitudes below 0.1 mag give the least reliable periods, and amplitudes below about 0.1-0.2 mag are generally fitted poorly.
- No amplitude comparison. Among LCDB advantages they list that dense light curves usually need no large or uncertain phase-angle corrections.
- They mention the difficulty of comparing spin amplitudes from different oppositions, while explaining why they do not compare colours across oppositions.

Others.
- Chang 2015: 65 LCDB matches, 13 period outliers. Chang 2016: 26 overlaps; 14 of 17 PTF-U2 periods agree to better than 3%. Neither compares amplitudes.
- Szabo 2022: no LCDB comparison.
- McNeill 2023: no per-object amplitude comparison; their Fig. 14 axis ratios explicitly assume no amplitude-phase-angle (PAA) correction.
- Vavilov & Carry: 78.5% full period agreement with Pal 2020. Amplitude against diameter is only plotted next to LCDB objects.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
- This is the most direct like-for-like quantity. LCDB AmpMin and AmpMax are the extremes of amplitudes from individual detail lines (one geometry each), so a per-apparition amplitude is the comparable quantity; an amplitude from all apparitions folded together is not.
- With 1000-8000 points over 8-34 years, many apparitions (especially ATLAS, ZTF, Pan-STARRS and Catalina) should have at least 20-50 points, which is the PTF regime.
- Risks: low S/N and phase gaps within single apparitions, magnitudes without reported errors, and TESS-via-MPC data rounded to 0.1 mag.
- PTF found amplitudes below about 0.1 mag unreliable.
- Knowing the period removes these surveys' main failure mode, aliasing.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. Split each asteroid's data into apparitions, either at gaps of 100 d or more (Cibulkova 2016) or in a window of about 1.1-1.6 yr centred on minimum alpha (Waszczak).
2. Within each apparition, keep the distance, light-time and HG1G2 reductions. Fit per-dataset zero points $Z_i$ (as in Chang Eq. 1), plus optionally a residual quadratic alpha term (as in Pal Eq. 1).
3. At the known period, fit a Fourier series of order K <= 4 with coefficients free per apparition. Choose K by F-test or BIC (as Vavilov & Carry do with F-tests). If the model shows a single maximum, treat it as a warning.
4. Compute A_app as the max-min of the model on a fine phase grid, with a bootstrap uncertainty. Require adequate phase coverage and A/sigma_A.
5. Rerun the existing injection test per apparition to calibrate the low-S/N bias of the K-term peak-to-peak (noise fitting inflates it). For apparitions with poor coverage, also compute the brightest-minus-faintest phase-bin amplitude (Szabo 2022).
6. Report max over apparitions of A_app (comparable to AmpMax), the median over apparitions, and the alpha-reduced versions from M2.
7. Validate as Pal 2020 did: histogram A_LCDB/A_ours over the overlap sample. Restrict the LCDB side to non-survey detail lines (see other_relevant_facts).
8. For data without errors, set the per-dataset sigma from the robust residual RMS, or use a Waszczak-style cosmic-error inflation until chi2/dof < 3.

methods.name: M2. Amplitude-phase-angle (PAA) correction after Zappala et al. (1990), optionally with an aspect-dependent ellipsoid amplitude
methods.data_type: Any amplitude measured at a known mean phase angle (dense, or per-apparition sparse)

methods.algorithm:
McNeill et al. 2019.
- Citing Zappala et al. (1990), they state a linear relation between apparent and zero-phase amplitude for alpha <= 40 deg.
- Eq. 24: $A(\alpha = 0^\circ) = \frac{A_{obs}}{1 + s\alpha}$, with s a taxonomy-dependent slope. With taxonomy unknown they adopt s = 0.015 mag deg^-1.
- Aspect dependence (Eq. 1, triaxial a > b >= c): $A_{obs} = -2.5\log\frac{b}{a} - 1.25\log\frac{a^2\cos^2\theta + c^2\sin^2\theta}{b^2\cos^2\theta + c^2\sin^2\theta}$. At theta = 90 deg this reduces to Eq. 2, $A_{obs} = -2.5\log\frac{b}{a}$.

Thirouin et al. 2016 (MANOS).
- Eq. 4 (from Binzel et al. 1989): $\Delta m = 2.5\log\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) - 1.25\log\left(\frac{a^2\cos^2\xi + c^2\sin^2\xi}{b^2\cos^2\xi + c^2\sin^2\xi}\right)$, where xi is the aspect angle between the rotation axis and the line of sight.
- Eq. 6: $\Delta m(\alpha=0^\circ) = \frac{\Delta m(\alpha)}{1+s\alpha}$. Eq. 7: $\frac{a}{b} \ge 10^{0.4\Delta m(\alpha)/(1+s\alpha)}$.
- They report that Zappala et al. (1990), from light curves of more than 30 asteroids, found s depends on taxonomic type: 0.013 mag deg^-1 (M), 0.015 (C), 0.030 (S).
- Numerical models by Gutierrez et al. (2006) give slopes that depend on topography and scattering, with an upper limit of 0.03. Thirouin adopt s = 0.03.

Lu & Jewitt 2019.
- Model: a biaxial ellipsoid (a > b = c) rotating about c, with Sun and observer in its equatorial plane, so the amplitudes are upper limits.
- Scattering: a Kaasalainen law, $S_{MK}(\alpha,\mu,\mu_0) = f(\alpha)\left(\frac{\mu\mu_0}{\mu+\mu_0} + C\mu\mu_0\right)$ with $f(\alpha) = A_0\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha}{D}\right) + K\alpha + 1$, fitted to Hapke parameters for C, S and V types.
- Amplitude: $\Delta m = 2.5\log\left(\frac{L_{max}}{L_{min}}\right)$ (Eq. 9). Results are given only as curves (Figs. 1-2) of amplitude against alpha up to 140 deg for a/b from 2 to 7.
- Findings: for small a/b, amplitude is proportional to alpha for alpha >~ 20 deg; below about 20 deg it is slightly non-linear because of the opposition effect.
- To first order the relation is independent of albedo and spectral type and depends mainly on shape.
- They describe Zappala's linearity as holding for alpha <= 50 deg, while McNeill says <= 40 deg.

Szabo et al. 2022, Eq. 1 (corrected attribution: the paper cites Magnusson 1986, not Zappala).
- $\frac{A(\varphi,\alpha)}{1+m\alpha} = 1.25\log\frac{(b/c)^2\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi}{(b/c)^2\cos^2\varphi + (b/a)^2\sin^2\varphi}$, for a > b > c.
- varphi is the aspect angle of the rotation axis. m is described as a parameter for the dependence on the phase function.
- A non-orthogonal aspect compresses the amplitude.

Chang et al. 2015, Eq. 5 (biaxial).
- $\Delta m = 2.5\log_{10}\left[\cos^2\theta + \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^2\sin^2\theta\right]^{-1/2}$, where theta is the angle between the line of sight and the spin vector.

Mommert et al. 2018.
- Ensemble estimate from the Zappala relation with an assumed average slope of 0.02 mag/deg and their sample's mean phase angle of 19 deg. On this basis they expected Gaia DR2 amplitudes to be overestimated by 40%.
methods.assumptions:
- Amplitude grows linearly with alpha up to 40 deg (McNeill) or 50 deg (Lu & Jewitt, describing Zappala).
- Lu & Jewitt's models show non-linearity below about 20 deg (opposition effect) and a slope that depends mainly on elongation.
- Zappala's slopes depend on class: 0.013 (M), 0.015 (C), 0.030 (S), as reported by Thirouin 2016. Gutierrez 2006 gives an upper limit of about 0.03.
- The ellipsoid formulas assume geometric scattering and principal-axis rotation about c.
methods.validation_reported:
- None of these papers validates the PAA correction directly against the LCDB.
- McNeill 2019, (18018): the observed 1.33 +/- 0.03 mag becomes 1.00 +/- 0.03 mag after correction. PTF single-opposition data (Waszczak 2015) gave 0.77 mag; McNeill reads this as the spin axis being inclined to the orbital plane.
- Thirouin 2016 (NEOs, alpha up to about 60 deg): the MANOS mean a/b drops from 1.54 to 1.23 with s = 0.03. This is not an LCDB comparison.
- Lu & Jewitt: qualitative comparisons with high-phase light curves (Saturn's irregular satellites, 'Oumuamua) only.
- Mommert 2018: expected a 40% PAA overestimate but found Gaia amplitudes about 51% too low against the LCDB. They concluded the phase-angle effect is insignificant for their ensemble analysis.
- Pal 2020: uses the PAA argument to explain the 7.6% median excess of LCDB over TESS amplitudes.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
- The correction is necessary but does not explain a deficit on its own.
- Our alpha spans about 3-35 deg, so the factor 1 + s*alpha at 35 deg is about 1.46 (M), 1.53 (C) or 2.05 (S); near 3 deg it is about 1.04-1.09.
- HG1G2 removal corrects only mean brightness, not amplitude growth, so mixing alpha mixes amplitudes that differ by tens of percent.
- Lu & Jewitt imply the linear law is least accurate in the alpha < 20 deg range where many survey points lie.
- Correction to the draft: the LCDB readme's lc_details column map has no phase-angle or PAB columns, only an approximate mid-date of observations (and details split by PAB or phase only where one paper reported changes). Reducing LCDB detail amplitudes to alpha = 0 therefore means computing alpha and aspect from ephemerides at that mid-date.
- Two consistent options remain: (a) reduce both sides to alpha = 0, or (b) compare at matched alpha.
methods.implementation_sketch:
Option A (post hoc).
- For each apparition, compute the data-weighted mean alpha and report A_app(0) = A_app/(1 + s*alpha), using s by class (0.013 M, 0.015 C, 0.030 S; Zappala via Thirouin 2016), or 0.015 when the class is unknown (McNeill).
- For the LCDB side, compute alpha at each detail line's mid-date from ephemerides and apply the same reduction.

Option B (in model).
- Within or across apparitions, scale the rotational Fourier term by (1 + s*(alpha - alpha_ref)), following the A/(1 + m*alpha) form of Szabo Eq. 1.
- Fit s per object when alpha coverage is wide; otherwise fix it.
- Evaluate the amplitude at alpha_ref = 0 or at the LCDB alpha.
- Option B is the researcher's extension of the published relation, not a published method.

For alpha < 20 deg, consider replacing the linear law with Lu & Jewitt-type model curves, i.e. a calibration table of amplitude against (a/b, alpha). This is a suggestion; the paper gives figures, not a closed form.

methods.name: M3. Amplitude from per-apparition brightness dispersion (variance or eta statistic) with noise subtraction
methods.data_type:
Sparse survey photometry where the period is unknown or not used:
- Cibulkova 2016: per apparition, with at least 20 points per apparition and at least 5 apparitions.
- Nortunen 2017: blocks of 3 days or less with at least 5 points.
- Mommert 2018: Gaia DR2, at least 5 transits.

Nortunen H., Kaasalainen M., Durech J., Cibulkova H. et al. 2017, A&A 601, A139 (doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629850), Shape and spin distributions of asteroid populations from brightness variation estimates and large databases

methods.algorithm:
Nortunen et al. 2017.
- Biaxial ellipsoid with p = b/a and b = c = 1.
- Eq. 1: $L = \sqrt{p^2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi + \sin^2\theta\sin^2\phi + \cos^2\theta} = \sqrt{1 + (p^2-1)\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi}$.
- Eq. 2, inverse amplitude in intensity: $A = L_{min}/L_{max}$, $A = \sqrt{\cos^2\theta + p^2\sin^2\theta} = \sqrt{1+(p^2-1)\sin^2\theta}$.
- Eq. 7: $\eta(\theta,p) := \Delta(L^2)/\langle L^2\rangle = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left[\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta(1-p^2)} - \frac{1}{2}\right]^{-1}$, with $\Delta(L^2)=\sqrt{\langle(L^2-\langle L^2\rangle)^2\rangle}$ and $0 \le \eta \le 1/\sqrt{2}$.
- Eq. 8: $\eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\left(\frac{1}{1-A^2} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}$, $A = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}\eta} + \frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}}$.
- If eta > 1/sqrt(2), A is imaginary and the estimate is omitted.
- Each eta uses at least 5 points within 3 days, with $\arccos(e_{sun}\cdot e_{earth}) \le 30^\circ$ (Eq. 13). Their simulations showed the phase-angle error to be negligible next to other error sources.

Cibulkova et al. 2016 (triaxial, c = 1, per apparition; apparitions separated by gaps of at least 100 d).
- Eq. 5: $L^2 = \frac{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi}{a^2} + \frac{\sin^2\theta\sin^2\phi}{b^2} + \cos^2\theta$.
- Eq. 6: $\langle L^2\rangle = 1 + \frac{1}{2}\sin^2\theta\left(\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2}-2\right)$.
- Eq. 7: $\eta = \frac{a^2-b^2}{\sqrt{8}}\left[\frac{a^2b^2}{\sin^2\theta} + \frac{1}{2}(a^2+b^2-2a^2b^2)\right]^{-1}$.
- Phase removal first: observed brightness is divided by $g\left[h\exp(-\alpha/d) - k\alpha + 1\right]\frac{1+\cos\alpha}{2}$ (Eq. 8).
- Noise subtraction for observed eta (added; this is the per-apparition step): Eq. 12, $\eta_{obs} = \sqrt{\eta^2 - \sigma^2_{L^2}} = \sqrt{\eta^2 - 4\sigma_L^2}$; Eq. 13, $\eta_{obs} = \sqrt{\eta^2 - 4\sigma_L^2 - \sigma^2_{model}}$ if $\eta \ge \sqrt{4\sigma_L^2+\sigma^2_{model}}$, else 0. They use $\sigma_{model}=0.06$.
- Link to LCDB amplitudes: $A_{mag} = 2.5\log\frac{L_{max}}{L_{min}}$ (Eq. 14) and $\eta_A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\left(\frac{1}{1-A^2} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}$ (Eq. 15), with $A = L_{min}/L_{max} = 10^{-0.4A_{mag}}$.
- Noise calibration: $\sigma_L = \left(\sqrt{\eta^2-\eta_A^2-\sigma_{model}^2}\right)/2$ (Eq. 16), set to 0 if $\eta \le \sqrt{\eta_A^2+\sigma^2_{model}}$. This was applied to 9698 LCDB asteroids to calibrate the noise against brightness: $\sigma_L = 0.07 + \frac{(L_{mean}-80)^2}{2\times 55\,000}$ for $L_{mean} < 80$, and 0.07 otherwise (Eq. 17), with $L = 10^{-0.4(M-15)}$.

Mommert et al. 2018 (Gaia DR2).
- Reduce as $G_{11}(\alpha) = G - 5\log_{10}r\Delta$, then correct for phase with literature G12 values (Veres 2015, otherwise Oszkiewicz 2011), drawing G12 1000 times by Monte Carlo.
- Take the weighted standard deviation of the resulting $H_G$ values.
- Correction: the paper is internally inconsistent. Sect. 3.2 says the averaged weighted standard deviation is adopted as the amplitude; the Fig. 1 caption defines the peak-to-peak lower limit as two standard deviations; the Table 1 note says the nominal value is peak-to-peak. The Fig. 1 example (79 Eurynome, 0.10 mag) matches 2 sigma.
- Objects whose H_G shows a linear trend with alpha (r^2 > 0.5 or p < 0.05) are rejected.
- Elongation from $b/a = 10^{-0.4 A}$.
methods.assumptions:
- Rotational phases are sampled randomly within each block or apparition, and the aspect is constant within it.
- Ellipsoidal geometric scattering, modelled at opposition.
- The noise level is known or modelled.
- Nortunen: the approach works when observational noise is low, at most about 0.05 mag.
- An incorrect phase slope inflates the dispersion (Mommert).
methods.validation_reported:
Mommert 2018 (against LCDB U = 3).
- Many small LCDB amplitudes (<= 0.25 mag) are overestimated, partly because of wrong G12 values.
- For larger amplitudes their linear fit implies a 51% underestimate, with 20% scatter about the slope. The offset does not depend on the number of observations.
- Each amplitude was then increased by 51%, with 20% Gaussian noise added, before modelling.

Cibulkova 2016.
- a/b from Lowell data against 765 DAMIT models: Pearson 0.48 and Spearman 0.61 on real data; 0.88 and 0.91 on synthetic DAMIT-based data.
- b/c is not recovered: 0.053 and 0.088 on real data, 0.35 and 0.38 on synthetic data.
- Their model gives higher a/b than DAMIT for D < 25 km, possibly because noise is underestimated for fainter objects.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
- Works on every apparition independently and is insensitive to period or phase-alignment errors.
- Each apparition has a single aspect, so it measures what dense light curves measure.
- Needs a noise model, since about 60% of the points lack errors. Estimate the per-dataset noise from short-timescale or fixed-period Fourier residuals.
- 0.1-mag rounding adds quantization variance.
- Errors in the reference phase curve or the dataset offsets add spurious variance.
- Researcher's derivation, not from the papers: for a sinusoid the peak-to-peak amplitude is $2\sqrt{2}\,\sigma$, so a '2 sigma' amplitude is low by $\sqrt{2}$ (factor 1.41), comparable to Mommert's empirical 1.51. Caveat: this holds only if Mommert's amplitude really is 2 sigma (Fig. 1 caption), not 1 sigma (Sect. 3.2 wording).
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. Per apparition, form the residuals r_j after the distance, light-time, phase and offset corrections.
2. Estimate the per-dataset noise variance sigma_n^2. Add (0.1 mag)^2/12 for rounded data (researcher's addition; standard uniform-quantization variance).
3. Then either (a) A_pp = 2*sqrt(2)*sqrt(var(r) - sigma_n^2) for near-sinusoidal light curves, or (b) the intensity route: L_j = 10^{-0.4 r_j}; eta = sqrt(<(L^2-<L^2>)^2>)/<L^2>; eta_A^2 = eta^2 - 4 sigma_L^2 - sigma_model^2 (Cibulkova Eq. 13); A from Nortunen Eq. 8; A_mag = -2.5 log10 A.
4. Use as a check on M1 for apparitions with poor phase coverage.
5. Calibrate the scale against the LCDB overlap with a linear fit plus scatter, as Mommert did.

methods.name: M4. Aspect-aware physical modelling across apparitions (per-apparition ellipsoid fit, or full lightcurve inversion), then prediction of the amplitude at any geometry
methods.data_type:
Multi-apparition sparse photometry, optionally with an LCDB period prior:
- Lowell: accuracy about 0.1-0.2 mag.
- ATLAS: at least 100 points per object after cleaning.

methods.algorithm:
Cibulkova et al. 2016.
- Brightness of a geometrically scattering triaxial ellipsoid (Connelly & Ostro 1984), Eq. 1: $L \propto \frac{\pi abc}{2}\left(\sqrt{e^TMe} + \frac{e^TMs}{\sqrt{s^TMs}}\right)$, with $M = \mathrm{diag}(1/a^2, 1/b^2, 1/c^2)$ (Eq. 2).
- At opposition, $L \propto \pi abc\sqrt{e^TMe}$ (Eq. 3), with $e = [\sin\theta\cos\phi, \sin\theta\sin\phi, \cos\theta]^T$ (Eq. 4).
- For each apparition the model and observed $\langle L^2\rangle$ and $\eta$ are compared via Eq. 9: $\chi^2 = \chi^2_\eta + w\chi^2_{L^2} = \sum_{app}\frac{(\eta_{model}-\eta_{obs})^2}{\sigma_\eta^2} + w\sum_{app}\frac{\left(\langle L^2_{model}\rangle/\overline{\langle L^2_{model}\rangle} - \langle L^2_{obs}\rangle/\overline{\langle L^2_{obs}\rangle}\right)^2}{\sigma^2_{L^2}}$. The normalizing denominators are means over all apparitions; w = 5 was found best.
- Grid search: lambda and beta in 5-deg steps, a in [1.1, 4] and b in [1, a] in steps of 0.1.
- Aspect per apparition: $\cos\theta_{mean} = v\cdot e_{mean}$ (Eq. 11).
- Combining Eqs. 6 and 7 gives Eq. 10: $\eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+b^2-2a^2b^2}\left[1-\frac{1}{\langle L^2\rangle}\right]$. Apparitions that are brighter on average (closer to pole-on) show smaller dispersion.

Durech et al. 2016 (corrected).
- Convex and triaxial-ellipsoid inversion (Kaasalainen et al. 2001) over a 2-100 h period interval.
- Optional LCDB prior: P +/- 5% for U = 3 or 3-, P +/- 10% for U = 2+.

Durech et al. 2020 (ATLAS).
- Period scan over 2-1000 h. LCDB prior: +/- 5% (U = 3, 3-), +/- 10% (U = 2+), +/- 20% (U = 2).
- Scattering: Lommel-Seeliger plus Lambert, with a phase function in exponential-linear form.
- Outliers beyond 2.5 rms of a linear-exponential phase-curve fit are removed (about 15% of points).

Once pole and shape are known, the amplitude at any aspect and alpha follows from the model, or for an ellipsoid from Szabo Eq. 1, McNeill 2019 Eq. 1 or Thirouin Eq. 4 (M2).
methods.assumptions:
- Constant sidereal period and spin axis.
- Convex or ellipsoidal shape and a chosen scattering law.
- Enough apparitions to span a range of aspects (Cibulkova: at least 5 apparitions with at least 20 points each).
- b/c is poorly constrained for high-latitude poles, because the range of aspect is limited.
methods.validation_reported:
Cibulkova 2016: see M3 (a/b correlation 0.48/0.61 on real data; b/c not determined).

Durech 2016:
- False-positive rate of a few percent against DAMIT, although the DAMIT comparison sample is itself biased against low-amplitude, long-period objects.
- Models from noisy sparse data are strongly biased toward elongated, high-amplitude bodies; almost all their models have amplitudes >~ 0.3 mag.
- Inversion works less well for poles near the ecliptic plane, which are seen nearly pole-on with small amplitudes in some apparitions; Hanus et al. 2011 put this bias at several tens of percent.

Durech 2020: about 2750 unique models from about 98,000 asteroids.

No amplitude-level comparison with the LCDB was found in any of these papers.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
- The most physically complete answer to what amplitude dense observers would have seen.
- Our 8-34 yr multi-apparition baselines with a known period match these inputs.
- The cost is an inversion per object, and the results are biased toward elongated shapes.
- The per-apparition (<L^2>, eta) approach is a lighter-weight alternative that uses the anticorrelation between mean brightness and amplitude (Eq. 10).
- Caveat: per-dataset magnitude shifts onto a reference phase curve can absorb apparition-dependent mean brightness (pole information) when a dataset spans one apparition. Colazo 2025 instead fit a separate H_i per apparition with shared G1 and G2.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. Use the LCDB period as a narrow prior (Durech-style) and run convex or ellipsoid inversion on the calibrated data, with per-dataset offsets as nuisance parameters.
2. For each LCDB detail line, take its mid-date (the only epoch information in lc_details), compute the geometry from ephemerides, synthesize the light curve, and compare peak-to-peak amplitudes. Otherwise compare the model's amplitude range over apparitions with AmpMin and AmpMax.
3. Cheaper path: grid-fit (lambda, beta, a, b) with Cibulkova Eq. 9 on per-apparition (<L^2>, eta), then predict the amplitude at each aspect, reduced in alpha via M2.

methods.algorithm:
Szabo & Kiss 2008.
- Eq. 2: $m(\phi) = m_0 + 1.25\log\left(\frac{\sin^2\vartheta\sin^2\phi}{a^2} + \frac{\sin^2\vartheta\cos^2\phi}{b^2} + \frac{\cos^2\vartheta}{c^2}\right)$. Eq. 3: $\Delta m_{1,2} = |m(\phi_1) - m(\phi_2)|$.
- Pairs are selected with a change of less than 2.5 deg in angle from opposition and less than 1.5 deg in phase angle.
- The observed CDF is fitted by non-negative least squares as a combination of Monte Carlo templates for 17 a/b values.

McNeill 2016.
- Eq. 8: $A = \pi\sqrt{c^2\sin^2\theta(a^2\sin^2\phi + b^2\cos^2\phi) + a^2b^2\cos^2\theta}$, where theta is the angle between the spin axis and the plane of the sky.
- Eq. 9: $\Delta m = |2.5\log\frac{A_1}{A_2}| = |m_1 - m_2|$, for pairs 900 s apart.
- Truncated-Gaussian b/a, arccos-distributed obliquity, and a two-sample KS test. Cuts: sigma <= 0.02 mag, alpha <= 10 deg.

Nortunen 2017 and Cibulkova 2018 (LEADER).
- $C(A) = \sum_{ij} w_{ij}F_{ij}(A)$, with $F_{ij}(A) = 0$ for $A \le p_i$; $\frac{\pi}{2} - \arccos\frac{\sqrt{A^2 - p_i^2}}{\sin\beta_j\sqrt{1-p_i^2}}$ for $p_i < A < \mathcal{F}(p_i,\beta_j)$; and $\pi/2$ for $A \ge \mathcal{F}$, where $\mathcal{F}(p_i,\beta_j)=\sqrt{\sin^2\beta_j + p_i^2\cos^2\beta_j}$.
- Note: beta here is measured from the pole (a co-latitude).
- Cibulkova 2018 cuts: points more than 0.01 d apart, alpha <= 20 deg, at least 5 points within 3 days.
methods.assumptions: Random rotational phases, ellipsoids, and a population-level spin distribution. No per-object amplitudes.
methods.validation_reported:
- Szabo & Kiss 2008: compared with a/b derived from the maximum amplitudes of 1207 asteroids with multi-epoch full light curves (Magnusson & Kryszczynska 2007). They report excellent agreement but give no metric.
- McNeill 2016: mean axis ratios 1 : 0.85 +/- 0.13 : 0.71 +/- 0.13.
- Mommert 2018 quotes these as 1 : 0.85 +/- 0.13 : 0.71 +/- 0.12, updated to 1 : 0.83 +/- 0.07 : 0.70 +/- 0.06 with a model that better accounts for the phase-angle amplitude effect.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
- Limited for per-object amplitudes.
- Useful framework: the amplitude seen in any one apparition is compressed by aspect (Nortunen Eq. 2), so a multi-apparition average falls below the equatorial-aspect amplitude.
- The maximum over apparitions is the analogue of the 'maximum amplitude' used by Szabo & Kiss.
methods.implementation_sketch:
Use only as a consistency check:
1. Simulate the actual sampling and aspects for ellipsoids under an assumed pole distribution.
2. Apply both the combined-fold estimator and the M1 per-apparition estimator.
3. Compare both with the single-epoch amplitudes from the same simulation. This gives the deficit expected from aspect averaging alone.

methods.algorithm:
SNAPS (ZTF, objects with more than 50 observations).
- Lomb-Scargle per filter, then Fourier models per filter to get g-r.
- g data are shifted by the colour onto r, and the period is refined.
- A final Fourier (LSP) model of the combined data gives the amplitude.

Gowanlock 2024 (ZTF plus TESS).
- ZTF records are offset using the mean TESS magnitude.
- Amplitudes come from the peak and trough of the sinusoidal fit. The authors note this generally underestimates amplitudes, but prefer it to raw max-min, which outliers inflate.

Erasmus 2021 (ATLAS plus ZTF).
- Correction: they use H-G with a generic G = 0.15, not a fitted phase curve.
- Filters are merged by subtracting colours, with o as the reference.
- A Fourier series is fitted to the folded data; amplitude = fit maximum minus minimum.
- Preselection: amplitude >~ 0.4 mag, via a standard deviation > 0.2 mag.

Erasmus 2026 (about 10 yr of ATLAS).
- Per-filter H,G fit with $\Phi_i(\alpha) = \exp\left[-A_i\tan^{B_i}(\alpha/2)\right]$ (Eq. 3), then Lomb-Scargle.
- Amplitude = max-min of a boxcar running average (window 10% of a cycle, wrapped) over the folded combined light curve, described as a conservative lower limit.
- Elongation: $a/b \ge 10^{0.4\Delta m}$ (Eq. 6), called a strict lower bound because it ignores both aspect and the amplitude-phase relation.

Empirical calibration.
- Mommert 2018: linear fit of their amplitudes against LCDB U = 3, giving the 1.51 factor with 20% scatter.
- Pal 2020: median of A_LCDB/A_survey.
methods.assumptions: The fold is coherent across apparitions, and aspect and phase-angle changes are ignored. The authors knowingly treat these amplitudes as lower limits.
methods.validation_reported:
SNAPS.
- Synthetic tests only: about 60% of amplitudes within 10% of the input, and 90% within about 20%.
- They explicitly do not compare amplitudes with the LCDB, because amplitudes can change from epoch to epoch with pole orientation.
- Spot checks: (1620) Geographos 1.14 mag (LCDB 1-2 mag); (1865) Cerberus 1.4 mag (LCDB 0.56-2.3 mag).

Others.
- Gowanlock: no LCDB amplitude comparison; excluding amplitudes <= 0.075 mag is one of the optimizations tested.
- Erasmus 2021 and 2026: no LCDB amplitude comparison.
- Mommert 2018: -51% with 20% scatter.
- Pal 2020: median ratio about 1.076.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
- This is the user's current situation. The literature treats folded multi-apparition amplitudes as lower limits; apart from Mommert's ensemble scaling, it does not try to equate them with LCDB values.
- The user's Fourier-4 injection result parallels the SNAPS synthetic test.
- An ensemble factor (A_lit approximately k * A_fold, with k about 1.33) is defensible for populations but not for individual objects.
methods.implementation_sketch:
If the combined fold is kept:
1. Label it an apparition-averaged amplitude, i.e. a lower limit.
2. Fit k by robust regression of LCDB amplitudes on A_fold. State whether AmpMax, AmpMin or the detail-line mean is used, and exclude Survey-flagged LCDB entries.
3. Report the scatter of k as the per-object uncertainty.

Preferred: replace or supplement the fold with M1 per-apparition amplitudes (plus the M2 alpha reduction).

verified.other_relevant_facts:
VERIFICATION SUMMARY
- Every cited arXiv id exists and matches the stated paper (checked through the arXiv API and full PDFs). Full texts of all papers in the methods were read and their equations checked against the PDFs.
- Journal references were confirmed from arXiv metadata, PDF headers or search results for: Pal 2020 (ApJS 247, 26), Szabo 2022 (A&A 661, A48), Gowanlock 2024 (AJ 168, 181), Erasmus 2020 (ApJS 247, 13), Durech 2016 (A&A 587, A48), Vavilov & Carry 2025 (A&A 693, A66), and Huang 2026 (PASP 138, 074401).
- The Novakovic & Gutierrez 2025 journal (stated as AJ in the draft) could not be confirmed and is dropped.

CORRECTIONS TO THE DRAFT
1. Pal 2020: full title corrected.
2. iPTF cadences: Chang 2015 used about 20 min over 4 nights; Chang 2016 about 10 min over 2-3 nights.
3. Vavilov & Carry: the order is the smallest k that no other k beats significantly in pairwise F-tests (95%). The period is doubled if the fit has only one local maximum; this is not a requirement of at least 2 maxima.
4. Szabo 2022 Eq. 1 cites Magnusson (1986), not Zappala. The Zappala relation is quoted by McNeill 2019, Thirouin 2016, Lu & Jewitt 2019, Mommert 2018, Pal 2020, McNeill 2023 and Erasmus 2026.
5. Durech 2016 scanned 2-100 h, with an LCDB prior only for U = 3, 3- and 2+. The 2-1000 h scan and the +/-20% prior for U = 2 are from Durech 2020.
6. Cibulkova 2016: the per-apparition noise subtraction is Eqs. 12-13. Eq. 16 is the LCDB-based noise calibration. Real-data b/c correlations are 0.053 and 0.088.
7. Mommert 2018 is internally inconsistent: Sect. 3.2 calls the standard deviation the amplitude, while the Fig. 1 caption defines amplitude as 2 sigma. The sqrt(2) argument depends on which is meant.
8. Erasmus 2021 used a fixed G = 0.15, not a fitted phase curve.
9. LCDB lc_details has no phase-angle or PAB fields, only an approximate mid-date; geometry must be computed from it.
10. McNeill 2016's axis ratios are 0.71 +/- 0.13 in their own abstract; Mommert quotes +/- 0.12.

ADDED: LCDB COMPOSITION (readme revised 2023 Oct 1)
- All amplitudes are peak-to-peak. AmpMin and AmpMax use only detail lines with U >= 2-.
- Survey results (sparse wide-field such as PTF and ZTF, dense wide-field such as TESS, sparse data, sparse lightcurve inversion) carry a Survey flag and are excluded from the BASIC DATA set. Lightcurve inversion that relies significantly on dense data (LCI-D) is the exception.
- By policy, most survey light curves with a claimed 'reliable' period are assigned U = 2.
- In the U >= 2- summary statistics based on AmpMax, 19,823 of 28,781 objects (68.9%) are Survey.
- Consequence: a comparison with LCDB AmpMax that does not filter on the Survey flag partly compares survey with survey (including Pal's TESS and Waszczak's PTF amplitudes).
- Pal 2020 used the Aug 2019 LCDB release, which predates the TESS entries.
- Details are split by approximate PAB or phase only when one paper reported changes; the readme gives the purpose as statistical studies of amplitude versus phase versus class.
- The readme gives the synodic-sidereal difference as DeltaP = [d(PAB)/dt] * P^2. Its example (P = 8 h, PAB changing 0.05 deg/day) gives 0.00037 h.

ADDED: ZAPPALA SLOPES BY CLASS
- As reported by Thirouin et al. 2016: M 0.013, C 0.015, S 0.030 mag/deg.
- Gutierrez et al. 2006 give an upper limit of about 0.03.
- Lu & Jewitt 2019 models: linear for alpha >~ 20 deg, non-linear below; shape-dependent and nearly type-independent.
- McNeill says Zappala's relation holds for alpha <= 40 deg, Lu & Jewitt say <= 50 deg.

RETAINED ANALYSIS (researcher's own inference, not from a paper)
- A fold of synodic data over 8-34 yr at one period can misalign the extrema across apparitions. With T = 30 yr and P = 8 h the fold requires dP/P << P/T, about 3e-5.
- A coherent injection test cannot detect this loss. Diagnostic: compare per-apparition amplitudes with the fold amplitude, and look for drift in the epoch of maximum.
- Pal's 7.6% LCDB excess for single-geometry TESS data suggests phase angle explains only part of a 25% deficit.
- Quantization from 0.1-mag rounding adds a variance of (0.1)^2/12, i.e. sigma of about 0.029 mag (standard statistics).

OTHER CHECKED FACTS
- Colazo 2025 (arXiv:2503.05412): no correction for amplitude or geometry. For NEAs, the per-apparition H differs by 0.22 mag on average and up to 0.6 mag. LCDB maximum amplitude (1 mag if none listed) is the rejection tolerance per 1-deg bin. Fits use a separate H_i per apparition with shared G1 and G2.
- Erasmus 2020 (arXiv:2002.08135, ApJS 247, 13), 262 LCDB overlaps: periods match within 1% for 76% and within 10% for 89% (alias periods counted); no amplitudes.
- Durech & Hanus 2023 (arXiv:2305.10798, A&A 675, A24) and Durech et al. 2019 (arXiv:1909.09395, A&A 631, A2): no amplitude validation found.
- Molnar et al. 2018 (arXiv:1706.06056): K2 amplitude and period distributions compared with the LCDB only as histograms.
- Podlewska-Gaca et al. 2021 (arXiv:2104.12403): periods only.
- Lindberg et al. 2022 (arXiv:2111.12596): amplitude as a Gaussian-process hyperparameter; the LCDB is used only as a period prior.
- Oszkiewicz et al. 2025 (arXiv:2511.16237): normalizes sparse photometry to pole-on geometry using Cellinoid, DAMIT or ISAM spin and shape models, i.e. the inverse of this problem.
- Novakovic & Gutierrez 2025 (arXiv:2509.06533): dense-photometry validation of super-fast-rotator candidates.
- Huang et al. 2026 (arXiv:2606.26184): KMTNet periods consistent with the LCDB.
- Takacs et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.13332): multi-epoch TESS ellipsoid inversion; not about amplitude correction.
