methods.name: Per-apparition normalized dispersion of squared intensity (eta) with photometric-noise subtraction, plus a triaxial-ellipsoid aspect model (Cibulkova et al. 2016, Lowell/MPC sparse data)
methods.data_type: Individual asteroids. Heterogeneous MPC sparse photometry recalibrated in the Lowell Observatory database: data from 11 observatories stored at the MPC, calibrated against SDSS (Oszkiewicz et al. 2011), accuracy about 0.1-0.2 mag. Many apparitions per object.

papers.citation: Cibulkova H., Durech J., Vokrouhlicky D., Kaasalainen M., Oszkiewicz D. A. 2016, A&A 596, A57, 'Distribution of spin-axes longitudes and shape elongations of main-belt asteroids' (DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201629192)

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED against the arXiv v1 full text. Eqs. 1-17 match, and the overlines in Eq. 9 were checked on the rendered page.

Model: a geometrically scattering triaxial ellipsoid, $a \ge b \ge c = 1$, rotating about the shortest axis.
- Eq. 1: $L \propto \frac{\pi abc}{2}\left(\sqrt{\mathbf{e}^T M \mathbf{e}} + \frac{\mathbf{e}^T M \mathbf{s}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{s}^T M \mathbf{s}}}\right)$
- Eq. 2: $M=\mathrm{diag}(1/a^2,1/b^2,1/c^2)$
- Eq. 3 (opposition, $\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{s}$): $L \propto \pi abc\sqrt{\mathbf{e}^T M \mathbf{e}}$
- Eq. 4: $\mathbf{e}=[\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta]^T$, with $\theta$ the aspect angle and $\phi$ the rotation angle.
- Eq. 5 ($c=1$, normalized by $\pi ab$): $L^2=\frac{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi}{a^2}+\frac{\sin^2\theta\sin^2\phi}{b^2}+\cos^2\theta$
- Eq. 6: $\langle L^2\rangle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}L^2\,d\phi=1+\frac{1}{2}\sin^2\theta\left(\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2}-2\right)$
- Eq. 7: $\eta=\frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{var}(L^2)}}{\langle L^2\rangle}=\frac{\sqrt{\langle(L^2-\langle L^2\rangle)^2\rangle}}{\langle L^2\rangle}=\frac{a^2-b^2}{\sqrt{8}}\left[\frac{a^2b^2}{\sin^2\theta}+\frac{1}{2}(a^2+b^2-2a^2b^2)\right]^{-1}$

Eqs. 6 and 7 are evaluated for each apparition. An apparition is a set of observations separated from the next set by a gap of at least 100 days.

Data steps:
1. Remove the phase-angle dependence by dividing the brightness by Eq. 8, $g\left(h\exp^{-\alpha/d}-k\alpha+1\right)\frac{1+\cos\alpha}{2}$, with g, h, d, k fitted per asteroid (after Hanus et al. 2011).
2. Require at least 20 points per apparition and at least 5 apparitions.
3. Normalize L by its mean over all apparitions (Fig. 1).

Fit, Eq. 9: $\chi^2=\chi^2_\eta+w\chi^2_{L^2}=\sum_{app}\frac{(\eta_{model}-\eta_{obs})^2}{\sigma^2_\eta}+w\sum_{app}\frac{(\langle L^2_{model}\rangle/\overline{\langle L^2_{model}\rangle}-\langle L^2_{obs}\rangle/\overline{\langle L^2_{obs}\rangle})^2}{\sigma^2_{L^2}}$
- Combining Eqs. 6 and 7 gives Eq. 10: $\eta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+b^2-2a^2b^2}\left[1-\frac{1}{\langle L^2\rangle}\right]$
- Mean aspect per apparition, Eq. 11: $\cos\theta_{mean}=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{mean}$, with $\mathbf{v}=[\cos\beta\cos\lambda,\cos\beta\sin\lambda,\sin\beta]^T$.
- Grid: lambda 0-360 deg and beta 0-90 deg in 5 deg steps; a from 1.1 to 4 and b from 1 to a, in steps of 0.1.

Noise removal (eta is the raw dispersion, eta_obs the corrected one):
- Eq. 12: $\eta_{obs}=\sqrt{\eta^2-\sigma^2_{L^2}}=\sqrt{\eta^2-4\sigma^2_L}$ if $\eta\ge 2\sigma_L$, else $\eta_{obs}=0$.
- With model noise, Eq. 13: $\eta_{obs}=\sqrt{\eta^2-4\sigma^2_L-\sigma^2_{model}}$ if $\eta\ge\sqrt{4\sigma^2_L+\sigma^2_{model}}$, else 0. Values 0.05, 0.06, 0.07 and 0.1 were tested; $\sigma_{model}=0.06$ was adopted.

Noise-level calibration against LCDB amplitudes:
- Eq. 14: $A_{mag}=2.5\log\frac{L_{max}}{L_{min}}=2.5\log\frac{L|_{\phi=0}}{L|_{\phi=\pi/2}}$
- Eq. 15: $\eta_A=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\left(\frac{1}{1-A^2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}$, with $A=L_{min}/L_{max}=10^{-0.4A_{mag}}$. This is the biaxial-ellipsoid relation; Nortunen et al. 2017 note it is not exact for a triaxial body.
- Eq. 16, computed for 9698 LCDB asteroids: $\sigma_L=\left(\sqrt{\eta^2-\eta^2_A-\sigma^2_{model}}\right)/2$ if $\eta>\sqrt{\eta_A^2+\sigma^2_{model}}$, else 0.
- A running mean of sigma_L over samples of 500 bodies against mean brightness gave Eq. 17: $\sigma_L=0.07+\frac{(L_{mean}-80)^2}{2\times 55\,000}$ for $L_{mean}<80$ and $\sigma_L=0.07$ for $L_{mean}>80$, where L is dimensionless, $L=10^{-0.4(M-15)}$.
methods.assumptions:
- Triaxial ellipsoid with geometric scattering; the model assumes opposition geometry, and the phase dependence is removed empirically with Eq. 8.
- Principal-axis rotation and uniform albedo.
- Aspect is constant within an apparition (mean aspect, Eq. 11), and rotational phases are randomly sampled within each apparition.
- Noise is Gaussian with known sigma_L and is subtracted in quadrature; residual model inadequacy is absorbed in sigma_model.
- Ambiguities: lambda vs lambda+180 deg, and only |beta| is recovered.
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED.

Synthetic data (DAMIT shapes with Hapke scattering on real Lowell geometries; noise 0.15 or 0.2 tested; the a/b test used 0.15):
- a/b recovered with Pearson 0.88 and Spearman 0.91.
- b/c recovered only at 0.35/0.38.

Real Lowell data against DAMIT models (765 asteroids):
- a/b: Pearson 0.48, Spearman 0.61.
- b/c: 0.053/0.088, so b/c is not determined.

Tuning on the DAMIT subset gave sigma_L = 0.08 and w = 5 as best. This produced almost no spheroids for fainter objects, hence the brightness-dependent noise of Eq. 17 calibrated on LCDB amplitudes.

Bootstrap (10 resamplings of the first 10,000 numbered asteroids; 9774 had enough data):
- a/b well determined (maximum spread <= 0.25) for 3819 asteroids, mean largest spread 0.18.
- lambda well determined (spread <= 50 deg) for 3930, mean largest spread 30 deg.
- Summary uncertainty about 0.2 in a/b and 30 deg in lambda.

Systematics:
- beta is biased toward high |sin beta|.
- For D < 25 km the method gives median a/b about 1.6. For D < 8 km, the DAMIT mean is 1.47 (biased toward elongated bodies) and McNeill et al. 2016 give 1:0.85 (a/b = 1.18).
- For D > 50 km the DAMIT mean is 1.23 and the model gives 1.29.
- The authors attribute the small-body excess to underestimated noise for faint objects.

Cibulkova et al. (2018), Sect. 5.2, and Mommert et al. (2018), Sect. 5.1, both repeat that underestimated (Lowell) noise makes shapes too elongated.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
Most directly applicable: it was designed for heterogeneous MPC-derived sparse photometry spanning many apparitions, which is our situation. Each apparition yields its own dispersion and amplitude estimate, so it avoids the main cause of our deficit (averaging light curves seen at different aspect and phase angles). The ellipsoid model (Eqs. 6, 7, 10, 11) links the apparitions through the aspect angle.

Weak points for us:
- (a) The noise must be known. 60% of our magnitudes lack uncertainties, and the paper's own experience is that underestimated noise inflates eta and the amplitudes.
- (b) Zero-point offsets between surveys within an apparition add to the dispersion.
- (c) The 0.1-mag rounding (TESS via MPC and others) adds a quantization variance.
- (d) The phase-angle dependence of the amplitude is not modelled; eta refers to the apparition's mean phase angle.
- (e) LCDB amplitudes are not phase-corrected.

With 1000-8000 points over 8-34 yr, the requirements of >= 20 points per apparition and >= 5 apparitions are usually met.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. After distance and light-time reduction and HG1G2 phase removal, split each asteroid's data into apparitions (gap >= 100 d). Within an apparition, re-center each survey on its own median when it has enough points; this removes zero-point leakage into eta. This step is ours, not the paper's.
2. Convert residuals to intensities $L_i=10^{-0.4\,\Delta m_i}$, normalize by the apparition mean, and compute $\eta=\mathrm{std}(L^2)/\mathrm{mean}(L^2)$, weighted if desired.
3. Per-point relative noise $\sigma_{L,i}\approx 0.921\,\sigma_{m,i}$. For datasets rounded to 0.1 mag, add $(0.1)^2/12$ to $\sigma_m^2$ (standard quantization variance, not from the paper). For datasets without uncertainties, estimate sigma_m per survey and magnitude bin from close pairs ($\mathrm{var}(\Delta m)/2$ for pairs minutes apart), or with Eq. 16 on a calibration set of LCDB U = 3 asteroids kept disjoint from the validation set.
4. Noise-corrected dispersion: $\eta_{corr}=\sqrt{\eta^2-4\langle\sigma_L^2\rangle-\sigma^2_{model}}$ (Eq. 13), set to 0 when the argument is negative. Use sigma_model = 0 for pure amplitude estimation, or 0.06 when fitting pole and shape as in the paper.
5. Convert to amplitude with the inverse of Eq. 15 (biaxial approximation): $A=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}\eta_{corr}}+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}}$, $A_{mag}=-2.5\log_{10}A$.
6. Optionally grid-fit (lambda, beta, a, b) with Eq. 9 over all apparitions. The equator-on amplitude $2.5\log(a/b)$ and the amplitude at any epoch (for example an LCDB observation date) then follow from Eqs. 5-7.
7. Compare the maximum over apparitions, or the model equator-on value, with LCDB AmpMax, and compare per-apparition values with LCDB detail lines from the same apparition.

methods.name: Analytic eta-to-amplitude conversion for a biaxial ellipsoid, and CDF inversion with aspect basis functions (Nortunen et al. 2017; LEADER, Nortunen & Kaasalainen 2017; applied to Pan-STARRS1 by Cibulkova et al. 2018)
methods.data_type: Population-level for the CDF inversion: about 1000 or more objects (LEADER requires N >~ 1000; Cibulkova 2018 finds b/a stable from about 800 objects). The eta-to-A conversion itself is per measurement set. Data used: WISE, ALCDEF and Pan-STARRS1 sparse data.

papers.citation: Nortunen H., Kaasalainen M., Durech J., Cibulkova H., Ali-Lagoa V., Hanus J. 2017, A&A 601, A139, 'Shape and spin distributions of asteroid populations from brightness variation estimates and large databases'
Nortunen H., Kaasalainen M. 2017, A&A 608, A91, 'LEADER: fast estimates of asteroid shape elongation and spin latitude distributions from scarce photometry' (DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201731360)

Cibulkova H., Nortunen H., Durech J., Kaasalainen M., Veres P., Jedicke R., et al. 2018, A&A 611, A86, 'Distribution of shape elongations of main belt asteroids derived from Pan-STARRS1 photometry' (DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201731554)

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED against the full texts.

Model: biaxial ellipsoid with $b=c=1$ and $p:=b/a$.
- Nortunen Eq. 1: $L=\sqrt{p^2\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi+\sin^2\theta\sin^2\phi+\cos^2\theta}=\sqrt{1+(p^2-1)\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi}$
- 'Inverse amplitude' $A=L_{min}/L_{max}$, Eq. 2: $A=\sqrt{\cos^2\theta+p^2\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{1+(p^2-1)\sin^2\theta}$
- Over one rotation: $\langle L^2\rangle=1+\frac{1}{2}\sin^2\theta(p^2-1)$ and $\Delta(L^2)=\sqrt{\langle(L^2-\langle L^2\rangle)^2\rangle}=\sin^2\theta(1-p^2)/\sqrt{8}$.
- Eq. 7: $\eta(\theta,p):=\Delta(L^2)/\langle L^2\rangle=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left[\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta(1-p^2)}-\frac{1}{2}\right]^{-1}$, with $0\le\eta\le 1/\sqrt{2}$.
- Hence Eq. 8: $\eta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\left(\frac{1}{1-A^2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}$ and $A=\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}\eta}+\frac{1}{2}\right)^{-1}}$. This is identical to LEADER Eq. 7 and Cibulkova 2018 Eq. 2.

In the biaxial model this relation holds at any aspect, so eta estimates and dense-light-curve amplitudes can be merged. Nortunen et al. state that no such simple conversion exists for a triaxial ellipsoid, where eta also depends on theta and b.

CDF for isotropic spins:
- Eqs. 3-4: $C(A)=\sum_i w_iF_i(A)$, with $F_i(A)=0$ for $A\le p_i$ and $F_i(A)=\sqrt{\frac{A^2-p_i^2}{1-p_i^2}}$ for $A>p_i$.
- From App. A, Eq. A.1: $\cos^2\theta_A(p)=\frac{A^2-p^2}{1-p^2}:=g_A(p)$; Eq. A.2: $C(A)=\int_0^A f(p)\sqrt{g_A(p)}\,dp$.

Observers near the ecliptic (App. A): substituting $\mathbf{e}=(\cos\lambda_e,\sin\lambda_e,0)$ gives $\cos\theta=\sin\beta\cos\Lambda$, with $\Lambda=\lambda-\lambda_e$ assumed isotropic and $\theta_{min}=\pi/2-\beta$. Here beta is the ecliptic polar angle (co-latitude) of the spin. This gives Eq. 6:
- $F_{ij}(A)=0$ for $A\le p_i$
- $\frac{\pi}{2}-\arccos\frac{\sqrt{A^2-p_i^2}}{\sin\beta_j\sqrt{1-p_i^2}}$ for $p_i<A<\mathcal{F}(p_i,\beta_j)$
- $\frac{\pi}{2}$ for $A\ge\mathcal{F}$, where $\mathcal{F}(p_i,\beta_j)=\sqrt{\sin^2\beta_j+p_i^2\cos^2\beta_j}$.

Inverse problem:
- Eq. 9: $Mw=C$.
- Eq. 10: $\hat w=\arg\min_w\{\|C-Mw\|^2+\delta_p\|R_pw\|^2+\delta_\beta\|R_\beta w\|^2\}$, $w\in\mathbb{R}^n_+$, solved by non-negative least squares (lsqnonneg).
- LEADER typical settings: $\delta_p=0.1$, $\delta_\beta=1$, grid $N_p=20$, $N_\beta=29$.

Measurement sets:
- Nortunen: at least 5 points within a 3-day window, and phase-angle limit Eq. 13, $\arccos(\mathbf{e}_{sun}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{earth})\le30^\circ$ (WISE).
- LEADER Eq. 2: $\alpha\le\alpha_{tol}$, with 20 deg for PS1.

LEADER phase handling per set:
- If $\min\alpha<8^\circ$, require (Eq. 3) $\max\alpha_i-\min\alpha_i\le1^\circ$; otherwise normalize by (Eq. 4) $\frac{L(\alpha)}{a\exp(b\alpha)}$.
- If $\min\alpha\ge8^\circ$, require (Eq. 5) a range $\le2^\circ$; otherwise use (Eq. 6) $\frac{L(\alpha)}{a\alpha+b}$.
- Complex or non-finite A (eta > 1/sqrt(2)) are discarded.

Cibulkova 2018 (PS1 w-band): consecutive measurements must be more than 0.01 d apart, alpha <= 20 deg, and at least 5 measurements within 3 days are required.
methods.assumptions:
- Biaxial (b = c) ellipsoid with geometric scattering in opposition geometry; brightness is proportional to projected area.
- Random rotational phase and constant aspect within a set (about 3 days).
- For the beta information, observers are concentrated near the ecliptic (LEADER: about 95% of observations within +/-20 deg of the ecliptic in their databases); spin longitudes are isotropic.
- No explicit noise subtraction. Nortunen et al. say noise enters the CDF as a convolution that they do not deconvolve, and that useful results need observational noise of 'at most 0.05 mag or so' (Sect. 6).
- The set must sample the rotation. Cibulkova 2018 find that b/a drifts toward 1 for P > 12 h with PS1, because most PS1 data for an asteroid were taken within a single night. They state this is a property of the PS1 cadence, not of the method.
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED with corrections.

Nortunen 2017:
- Analytic estimate for a boxcar-like signal: the average error of eta drops from about 50% with two points to close to 10% with five or six points.
- Simulations with DAMIT shapes, Lommel-Seeliger+Lambert scattering and real WISE geometries, using populations of 1000 objects: the peak location is recovered, but the p-peak is systematically shifted about 0.1 toward elongated values (noise and shape irregularity). This is corrected by a shift Delta P = 0.1.
- CORRECTION: the earlier statement that 'at least 500 objects are needed' is not in Nortunen 2017. Nortunen used populations of 1000; LEADER requires N >~ 1000 and reaches a fit error below 1% for 1000-2000 objects; Cibulkova 2018 find that b/a is stable from about 800 objects and that beta is unrecoverable below 500.

Cibulkova 2018 (synthetic data with 1-2% Gaussian noise and P from 3-12 h):
- Accurate b/a peak for populations above 1000 when b/a > 0.5.
- For P > 12 h the solution drifts toward b/a about 1.
- Real PS1: b/a peak about 0.8 for D < 25 km. They contrast this with about 0.63 from Cibulkova 2016 (Lowell) and note that the Lowell result could be affected by underestimated noise.
- Method bias puts the b/a values of the 4-8 h and 8-15 h period groups about 0.15 apart.
- They could not reproduce the McNeill et al. 2016 size trend using all measurements, and suggest McNeill's <= 0.02 mag error cut as the reason.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
Eq. 8 is the exact, model-consistent (biaxial) way to turn a per-apparition dispersion into an LCDB-style peak-to-peak amplitude, including for large amplitudes where a simple rms-times-constant rule is inaccurate. For small amplitudes it reduces to $A_{mag}\approx 2\sqrt{2}\,\sigma_m$ (our derivation; see other facts).

The CDF inversion is population-level and gives no per-object amplitudes. Its App. A geometry ($\cos\theta=\sin\beta\cos\Lambda$) describes how one object's per-apparition amplitude changes with the ecliptic longitude of observation, which is exactly what our multi-apparition fold averages over.

The 3-day windows would discard most of our data. Nortunen et al. (Sect. 6) state that, for main-belt asteroids, sparse points from one apparition can be combined for eta if a solar-phase correction is applied (Kaasalainen 2004; Durech et al. 2009; Cibulkova et al. 2016). That supports per-apparition sets.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. For each apparition (or shorter windows if the aspect changes a lot), compute $\eta=\mathrm{std}(L^2)/\mathrm{mean}(L^2)$ from phase-corrected intensities.
2. Subtract the noise contribution with Cibulkova 2016 Eq. 12/13 (LEADER has no noise subtraction).
3. Convert: $A=\sqrt{1-(1/(\sqrt{8}\eta)+1/2)^{-1}}$ and $A_{mag}=-2.5\log_{10}A$.
4. To interpret the spread over apparitions for one object, use Eq. 2 with $\cos\theta=\sin\beta\cos\Lambda$. The per-apparition A ranges from $p$ (equator-on, at $\Lambda=90^\circ$) to $\sqrt{\sin^2\beta+p^2\cos^2\beta}$. So $\min_{app}A$ (the largest magnitude amplitude) estimates $2.5\log(1/p)$, but only if one apparition is near equator-on. This is comparable to LCDB AmpMax.
5. A 2-parameter (p, beta) fit of the per-apparition A values against the known ecliptic longitudes of observation is a light version of the Cibulkova 2016 fit.
6. LEADER (per the paper, downloadable from the DAMIT software page) can check that our ensemble of per-apparition A values is consistent with published population b/a distributions (PS1: peak about 0.8 for D < 25 km).

methods.name: Lower-limit amplitude from twice the weighted standard deviation of phase-corrected sparse magnitudes, with an empirical LCDB calibration (Mommert et al. 2018, Gaia DR2)
methods.data_type: Individual asteroids. Sparse Gaia DR2 G-band transits (at least 5, median 9 per object), about 2 yr baseline, mean phase angle about 19 deg with a range of about 6 deg.

papers.citation: Mommert M., McNeill A., Trilling D. E., Moskovitz N., Delbo M. 2018, AJ 156, 139, 'The Main Belt Asteroid Shape Distribution from Gaia Data Release 2' (DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/aad338)

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED.

1. Reduced magnitude $G_{11}(\alpha)=G-5\log_{10}r\Delta$.
2. Phase correction with literature H-G12 slope parameters: Veres et al. 2015 if based on at least 5 observations (56% of objects), otherwise Oszkiewicz et al. 2011 (44%).
3. Monte Carlo over the G12 uncertainties, 1000 runs. Asymmetric errors are drawn from two Gaussians for the upper and lower 1-sigma values.
4. In each run, compute the normalized absolute magnitudes H_G and their weighted standard deviation, with weights equal to the inverse-square Gaia photometric uncertainties. Average over runs.
5. Definition of the amplitude. Sect. 3.2 calls this average weighted standard deviation 'the target's lightcurve amplitude'. The Fig. 1 caption defines the peak-to-peak lower-limit amplitude as two times the standard deviation, and Table 1 gives the 'nominal peak-to-peak value'. The Eurynome example (0.10 mag; dashed +/-1-sigma lines at about +/-0.058 mag in Fig. 1) is consistent with $A_{low}=2\,\sigma_w(H_G)$, so the 2-sigma reading is adopted. The Sect. 3.2 wording is loose.
6. Reject objects with residual linear trends against phase angle ($r^2>0.5$ or $p<0.05$).
7. Shape: $b/a=10^{-0.4\cdot A}$.
8. Population model: the McNeill et al. (2016) model with a chi-square test. In each Monte Carlo run every measured amplitude is increased by 51% and 20% relative Gaussian noise is added.
methods.assumptions:
- The phase curve (G12) is known from the literature.
- Light-curve scatter dominates the photometric noise; no noise is subtracted.
- 2 sigma is a lower limit because of incomplete sampling.
- The phase-angle effect on amplitude is neglected. Using Zappala et al. 1990 with 0.02 mag/deg at the mean alpha of 19 deg, they estimate a 40% overestimate, but conclude from the LCDB comparison that the effect is insignificant for the ensemble.
- b = c.
- Spin poles follow the Hanus et al. (2011) distribution for D <= 30 km; a uniform pole distribution gave results within 1 sigma.
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED. Compared with LCDB amplitudes of quality U = 3:
- For A_LCDB <= 0.25 mag, a significant fraction is overestimated. They attribute this partly to wrong G12 slopes and to brightness modulation with ecliptic longitude.
- For A_LCDB > 0.25 mag, a linear fit shows the derived amplitudes underestimate LCDB by 51% (corrected by multiplying by 1.51), with 20% scatter about that slope.
- The offset does not depend on the number of observations, although amplitudes from many observations are more reliable.
- Example: (79) Eurynome has a lower limit of 0.10 mag from 36 observations against an LCDB maximum of 0.25 mag.
- Results: b/a = 0.80 +/- 0.04 overall and 0.86 +/- 0.05 for D >= 50 km.
- Mommert et al. attribute the more elongated Cibulkova 2016 shapes to the large Lowell photometric uncertainties (0.1-0.2 mag), which can inflate amplitudes.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
Simple and robust. It is the closest published analogue of an 'rms of the residuals' estimator with an explicit LCDB comparison.

Note (our derivation): for a sinusoid the peak-to-peak amplitude is $2\sqrt{2}\,\sigma\approx2.83\sigma$, so 2 sigma alone should underestimate by a factor of 1.41. The empirical factor 1.51 (giving 3.02 sigma) is close to that. This suggests that $2\sqrt{2}\sigma$ per apparition, after noise subtraction, should be nearly unbiased against LCDB for A > 0.25 mag. Caveats: the Gaia sigma was not noise-subtracted and includes G12 errors, and the 1.51 comes from a linear fit restricted to A_LCDB > 0.25 mag.

For our data:
- (i) MPC noise (often 0.1-0.2 mag, much larger than Gaia's) must be subtracted in quadrature, or low amplitudes will be strongly overestimated.
- (ii) Compute it per apparition, not over 8-34 years; a long-baseline rms mixes the aspect-dependent mean brightness (apparition-to-apparition offsets) into the variance.
- (iii) The 1.51 factor is specific to Gaia DR2 sampling and should be recalibrated on our own LCDB overlap sample.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. For each apparition k, compute $s_k^2=\mathrm{wvar}(\Delta m)$, the weighted variance of the phase-corrected, survey-re-centered residuals.
2. Subtract noise: $\hat\sigma^2_{rot,k}=s_k^2-\langle\sigma^2_{noise}\rangle_k$. Include $0.1^2/12$ for rounded data, and use a per-survey noise estimate where uncertainties are missing.
3. Amplitude: $A_k=2\sqrt{2}\,\hat\sigma_{rot,k}$, or, following Mommert, $A_k=2\hat\sigma_{rot,k}\times c$ with c fitted on LCDB U = 3 objects.
4. Bootstrap within each apparition for uncertainties.
5. Report $\max_k A_k$ (bias-corrected by bootstrap) and the median.
6. Compare with LCDB AmpMax and AmpMin; fit the calibration slope of A_LCDB against A_k as Mommert did, and check its dependence on the number of points per apparition.

methods.name: Random-rotational-phase likelihood: arcsine (sinusoid) magnitude distribution convolved with Gaussian noise, fitted per opposition with MCMC (Schemel & Brown 2021, ZTF Jupiter Trojans)
methods.data_type: Individual objects. Sparse ZTF g and r detections (more than 10 per object; 1 June 2018 - 13 Aug 2020), 2-3 oppositions.

papers.citation: Schemel M., Brown M. E. 2021, Planet. Sci. J. 2, 40, 'Zwicky Transient Facility Observations of Trojan Asteroids: A Thousand Colors, Rotation Amplitudes, and Phase Functions' (DOI 10.3847/PSJ/abc752)

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED against arXiv v1; Eq. 6 was checked on the rendered page.

- Eq. 1, predicted non-rotating magnitude: $m_p=H_r+c-2.5\log_{10}[\phi(\alpha)]+5\log_{10}[R\Delta]$
- H-G phase function, Eq. 2: $\phi(\alpha)=(1-G)\phi_1(\alpha)+G\phi_2(\alpha)$; Eq. 3: $\phi_i=\exp[-A_i\tan^{B_i}\frac{1}{2}\alpha]$, with $A_1=3.33$, $A_2=1.87$, $B_1=0.63$, $B_2=1.22$.
- Noise, Eq. 4: $P_g(m|m_p,\sigma)=\exp\left[\frac{-(m_p-m)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]$
- Light curve, Eq. 5: $m=\frac{A}{2}\sin(p)+m_p$, with A the peak-to-peak amplitude and p the unknown rotational phase.
- Distribution over a rotation, as printed in arXiv v1 (Eq. 6): $P_r(m|m_p,A)=\frac{1}{(A/2)^2-(m-m_p)^2}$ (unnormalized). The arcsine density of a sinusoid is proportional to $1/\sqrt{(A/2)^2-(m-m_p)^2}$, so the square root appears to be missing in the printed v1.
- Eq. 7: $P(m|m_p,A,\sigma)=P_r(m|m_p,A)\circledast P_g(m|m_p,\sigma)$, truncated at each detection's 5-sigma limiting magnitude and renormalized.
- Outliers: points more than 1.5 mag from a preliminary prediction (JPL H, G = 0.15, mean g-r) are removed first. A spurious fraction f per magnitude enters Eq. 8: $\mathcal{L}(m_p,A,\sigma|m)=(1-f\Delta m)P(m|m_p,A,\sigma)+f$.
- A separate amplitude A_k and magnitude offset per opposition: H_r is referenced to 2019, and offsets off1 and off3 have Gaussian priors N(0, 0.1). A single G and a single g-r are fitted.
- Priors: uniform in -0.25 < G < 1.0, -1.5 < g-r < 1.5 and 0 < A < 2; H_r Gaussian centred on M_JPL + 0.04 with sigma 0.5; $p(f)=\cos(f\pi/2)^{10}$ with f < 0.33.
- Sampler: emcee affine-invariant, 30 walkers, 5000 steps, first 1000 discarded.
methods.assumptions:
- Sinusoidal light curve with constant amplitude within an opposition.
- The rotational phase of each detection is independent and uniform, so no period is needed.
- Gaussian measurement errors with known sigma.
- H-G phase function.
- The amplitude may change between oppositions (aspect change), and the mean-magnitude offsets between oppositions are small.
- The authors call the constant-amplitude assumption 'clearly unsatisfactory' for closer populations such as main-belt asteroids.
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED with one correction.

Individual Trojans:
- (11351) Leucus: 0.73 +/- 0.11 and 0.61 +/- 0.07, against Mottola et al. (2020) values of 0.65 (2018) and 0.7 mag (2019).
- (3548) Eurybates: upper limits of 0.18 and 0.15, against 0.1 mag (Mottola, private communication).
- (21900) Orus: 0.10 +/- 0.05, against 0.14 mag (2019).

Population:
- CORRECTION: the well-measured Kepler/K2 Trojan amplitudes (Szabo et al. 2017; Ryan et al. 2017) have mean values 'approximately 50% larger' than theirs, so the ZTF amplitudes are about 2/3 of K2, not 50% smaller.
- The authors attribute this to the sinusoid assumption. A test light curve with peaks of 0.25 and 0.1 mag returned 0.1, and they conclude that their amplitudes should be read as the smaller of a two-amplitude light curve.

Colors: agreement with SDSS for 156 Trojans, with a normalized-difference sigma of 1.08.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
Highly applicable as a statistically principled replacement for 'max-min of folded data'. It needs no folding, gives a per-apparition amplitude with uncertainty, naturally includes heteroscedastic noise and outliers, and handles upper limits.

Adaptations needed:
- (a) For datasets without uncertainties, make sigma a free per-survey (and magnitude-dependent) nuisance parameter shared across asteroids, or fix it from a calibration.
- (b) For 0.1-mag rounding, convolve additionally with a uniform kernel of width 0.1 mag.
- (c) Use per-survey zero-points within an apparition as nuisance parameters with Gaussian priors, instead of one offset per opposition.
- (d) Replace the sinusoid by an ellipsoid or two-harmonic shape to avoid the 'smaller peak' bias they report, for example the distribution of $L=\sqrt{1+(p^2-1)\sin^2\theta\cos^2\phi}$ in magnitudes, computed numerically. Alternatively, calibrate the sinusoid-A against LCDB.
- (e) The detection-limit truncation can be dropped for bright, well-detected main-belt asteroids.

Main-belt aspect changes within an apparition are larger than for Trojans, so shorter windows (per month or per alpha range) may be needed.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. For each asteroid and apparition k, the parameters are {A_k, mbar_k, survey offsets o_{s,k} ~ N(0, tau)}. Global parameters are {G1, G2, or a fixed phase curve from the main pipeline; sigma_s for surveys without errors; f}.
2. Likelihood per point: $\mathcal{L}_i=(1-f\Delta m)\,[P_r(\cdot|A_k)\circledast\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_i^2)\circledast U(-q/2,q/2)](m_i-\hat m_i)+f$, with the correctly normalized arcsine density $P_r(x)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{(A_k/2)^2-x^2}}$ for $|x|<A_k/2$. Evaluate the convolution on a grid, or analytically through the arcsine characteristic function $J_0$.
3. Sample with emcee, or maximize and use a Laplace approximation for speed.
4. Output the posterior of A_k per apparition. LCDB-comparable summaries are the posterior of $\max_k A_k$, or of the equator-on amplitude from an aspect fit (see the Cibulkova and Nortunen methods).
5. Validate on our LCDB U = 3 overlap and with injected light curves of realistic two-peak shapes.

methods.name: Flux-space variability semi-amplitude with marginalization over unknown light-curve phase, plus a population likelihood q(A) (Bernardinelli et al. 2023, DES TNOs)
methods.data_type: Individual objects and populations. Very sparse multi-band photometry (typically 8 epochs per band over 5-6 yr) with accurate per-epoch flux errors.

papers.citation: Bernardinelli P. H., Bernstein G. M., Jindal N., et al. (DES Collaboration) 2023, ApJS 269, 18, 'Photometry of Outer Solar System Objects from the Dark Energy Survey I: photometric methods, light curve distributions and trans-Neptunian binaries' (DOI 10.3847/1538-4365/acf6bf)

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED (Sect. 4-5).

- Eq. 7, model: $\hat f_j=\bar f_{b_j}[1+Ah(\phi_j)]$, with $\langle h\rangle=0$ and $\max_\phi h-\min_\phi h=2$, so A is the semi-amplitude of the fractional flux variation. The peak-to-peak magnitude is $\Delta m\equiv2.5\log_{10}(1+A)/(1-A)$. They take $h(\phi)=\sin(2\pi\phi)$ and assume the variation is achromatic.
- Eq. 8: $p(\{f_j\}|\{\bar f_b\},A,\{\phi_j\})\propto\prod_j\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{f_j-\bar f_{b_j}[1+Ah(\phi_j)]}{\sigma_j}\right)^2\right]$
- Observations within 1 hour share an unknown phase, forming sets s. Eq. 9: $p(\{f_j\}|\{\bar f_b\},A)\propto\prod_s\int_0^1 d\phi_s\prod_{j\in s}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{f_j-\bar f_{b_j}[1+Ah(\phi_s)]}{\sigma_j}\right)^2\right]$. The integral is computed as a sum over about 20 phase samples.
- Priors are uniform on $\bar f_b$ and on $0\le A<1$. Eq. 10: posterior $\propto$ likelihood, sampled by Metropolis-Hastings MCMC.
- Points more than 3 sigma outside the model span at the median A are clipped and the MCMC is re-run; every exposure is visually vetted.
- Population: the amplitudes are drawn from $q(A|\theta_A)$, for example a beta distribution $q(A|a,b)\propto A^{a-1}(1-A)^{b-1}$, using the per-object posterior samples, so non-detections enter rigorously.
methods.assumptions:
- Random, independent light-curve phases between groups: the period is unknown and short compared with the group spacing.
- Sinusoidal phase function. The authors say it is likely inaccurate for non-ellipsoidal shapes and use A only as an indicative variability measure.
- Accurate per-epoch errors; the authors stress that the A inferences depend critically on them.
- Achromatic variability and fixed geometry (TNOs).
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED.
- Eris: A constrained to 0.020-0.025 (68%), against a sinusoidal A = 0.015 +/- 0.001 from Bernstein et al. (2023). Spurious fluctuation sources (calibration, phase variation, systematics, underestimated errors) induce 'perhaps an extra 0.01 mag' of perceived variability semi-amplitude.
- (612620) 2003 SQ317: inferred A of about 0.2 (Delta m = 0.44 mag), against about 0.85 mag peak-to-peak from Lacerda et al. (2014). The discrepancy is attributed at least partly to the strongly non-sinusoidal (contact-binary-like) light curve, and possibly to a changing aspect.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
Same family as Schemel & Brown, but formulated in flux, with explicit grouping of near-simultaneous exposures. This suits ATLAS quads, PS1 tracklets and Catalina sequences, which are taken within about 1 h.

For main-belt periods of a few hours, the 'same phase within 1 h' assumption should be replaced by the known relative phase $\Delta t/P$ (we know P), keeping only one unknown phase per night or group.

Their two caveats map directly onto our problem: a misspecified error model inflates A (about +0.01 in semi-amplitude for Eris), and non-sinusoidal shapes bias A low relative to dense peak-to-peak values. The q(A) machinery could compare our per-apparition amplitude distribution with LCDB-like distributions while handling upper limits.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. Per apparition, group points by night (or by Delta t < P/20).
2. Model $f_j=\bar f_{s(j)}(1+A\,h(\phi_g+2\pi\Delta t_j/P))$, using the known P inside a group and one free phase $\phi_g$ per group, marginalized on a 20-50 point grid.
3. $\bar f$ carries per-survey multiplicative zero-points.
4. Take sigma_j from reported errors, inflated per survey by a fitted factor; where errors are missing, use a per-survey free parameter.
5. Sample (A, offsets, noise scalings) by MCMC and convert to $\Delta m=2.5\log_{10}\frac{1+A}{1-A}$.
6. A 2-harmonic template for h (fixed shape, scaled) should reduce the bias toward the smaller peak.

methods.name: Two-epoch magnitude differences of SDSS MOC pairs and statistical (template CDF + NNLS) inversion to an a/b distribution (Szabo & Kiss 2008)
methods.data_type: Population-level. Pairs of sparse SDSS MOC r-band detections (11,735 pairs; asteroids of about 1-30 km).

papers.citation: Szabo Gy. M., Kiss L. L. 2008, Icarus 196, 135, 'The shape distribution of asteroid families: evidence for evolution driven by small impacts'

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED.

1. Pair selection: change of opposition angle < 2.5 deg, change of solar phase < 1.5 deg, separation > 1 day (uncorrelated rotational phases), r < 20.
2. Distance reduction, Eq. 1: $\Delta m^{obs}_{1,2}=|m_1-5\log(D_1R_1)-m_2+5\log(D_2R_2)|$. Residual geometric effects are below about 0.02 mag.
3. Ellipsoid light curve, Eq. 2: $m(\phi)=m_0+1.25\log\left(\frac{\sin^2\vartheta\sin^2\phi}{a^2}+\frac{\sin^2\vartheta\cos^2\phi}{b^2}+\frac{\cos^2\vartheta}{c^2}\right)$, with vartheta the aspect angle.
4. Model observable, Eq. 3: $\Delta m_{1,2}=|m(\phi_1)-m(\phi_2)|$, with independent uniform phi_1 and phi_2.
5. Observed CDF, Eq. 4: $\xi(\Delta m_{1,2})=\frac{1}{\mathrm{number_{all}}}\mathrm{number}(\Delta m^{obs}_{1,2}<\Delta m_{1,2})$.
6. Template CDFs from 10^6 Monte Carlo pairs for each of 17 values of a/b: 1.1-2.0 in steps of 0.1, 2.2-3.0 in steps of 0.2, then 3.5 and 4.0.
7. The observed CDF is fitted as a non-negative least-squares (Lawson & Hanson) combination of the templates; the coefficients give the a/b distribution.
8. Aspect: vartheta = 90 deg for all objects, with an alternative solution using a random pole longitude and the latitude fixed at 50 deg.
methods.assumptions:
- Triaxial ellipsoid rotating about c, with geometric projection.
- Fixed aspect: 90 deg, or pole latitude 50 deg.
- Independent rotational phases.
- Negligible photometric noise (SDSS 1-2% to r = 20, checked with a KS test of bright against faint objects); no noise deconvolution.
- Robustness check: clipping Delta m > 0.65 left the second peak in place.
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED. The a/b distribution of the 11,735 SDSS pairs was compared with a/b from the maximum amplitudes of 1207 asteroids with multi-epoch published light curves (Magnusson & Kryszczynska 2007). The authors call the agreement 'excellent', qualitatively and without a number. They note that the maximal observed amplitude corresponds to perpendicular aspect and so approximates a/b. Coefficient uncertainties are below +/-3% per bin.

Later critiques (verified in the citing papers):
- McNeill et al. 2016: the a/b >= 1.1 grid imposes b <= 0.91a, leaving a dearth of near-spherical objects.
- Cibulkova et al. 2016 and 2018: the fixed-aspect assumption probably influenced the results.
- Nortunen et al. 2017, App. B: two-point observables give no recoverable beta information and are inferior to eta. Their basis functions G_i(q) are double integrals evaluated numerically, the 'closed-form' counterparts of the Szabo & Kiss Monte Carlo templates.
methods.applicability_to_our_data: Low for per-object amplitudes: this is a population method, and two-point statistics are the least informative observable. It is useful to us only as (a) a cross-check of our per-apparition amplitude distribution against an independent sparse-data population result, and (b) a demonstration that, after strict geometric matching of pairs, the residual scatter is dominated by rotation. Its validation also illustrates that maximum multi-epoch amplitudes, not averages, are the quantity to compare with equator-on shape.
methods.implementation_sketch:
Optional diagnostic only, not recommended as the primary amplitude estimator:
1. For each asteroid, draw pairs within an apparition: Delta alpha < 1.5 deg, Delta t > 1 d, same survey (avoids zero-point differences).
2. Build the CDF of |Delta m| over a population.
3. Compare with Monte Carlo templates from Eq. 2 using an isotropic aspect rather than a fixed 90 deg.

methods.name: Forward-modelled distributions of magnitude changes between consecutive detections, or of individual phase-corrected detections, compared with synthetic ellipsoid populations (McNeill et al. 2016, 2019, 2021; 'Extreme asteroids' 2018)
methods.data_type:
Population-level:
- Pan-STARRS1 detection pairs about 15 min apart (2016).
- Spitzer and PS1 partial light curves of NEOs (2019).
- ATLAS sparse detections of Jupiter Trojans (2021).

papers.citation: McNeill A., Fitzsimmons A., Jedicke R., Wainscoat R., Denneau L., Veres P., et al. 2016, MNRAS 459, 2964, 'Brightness variation distributions among main belt asteroids from sparse light curve sampling with Pan-STARRS 1' (DOI 10.1093/mnras/stw847)

McNeill A., Hora J. L., Gustafsson A., Trilling D. E., Mommert M. 2019, AJ 157, 164, 'Constraining the Shape Distribution of Near-Earth Objects from Partial Light Curves' (DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/ab0e6e)

McNeill A., Erasmus N., Trilling D. E., Emery J. P., Tonry J. L., et al. 2021, PSJ 2, 6, 'Comparison of the physical properties of the L4 and L5 Trojan asteroids from ATLAS data' (DOI 10.3847/PSJ/abcccd)

McNeill A., Fitzsimmons A., Jedicke R., Lacerda P., Lilly E., et al. 2018, AJ 156, 282, 'Extreme Asteroids in the Pan-STARRS 1 Survey' (DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/aaeb8c; the arXiv v1 header says 'Submitted to ApJ')

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED.

McNeill 2016:
- Detections with formal error <= 0.02 mag and alpha <= 10 deg; magnitude change between consecutive detections about 900 s apart.
- Projected area, Eq. 8: $A=\pi\sqrt{c^2\sin^2\theta(a^2\sin^2\phi+b^2\cos^2\phi)+a^2b^2\cos^2\theta}$, with theta the angle between the spin axis and the plane of the sky.
- Eq. 9: $\Delta m=|2.5\log\frac{A_1}{A_2}|=|m_1-m_2|$.
- Synthetic population: spin frequency uniform in 1-10.9 d^-1; obliquity from the arccos of a uniform deviate; b/a and c/b from truncated Gaussian or Lorentzian distributions; uniform error U(-0.02, 0.02) on each magnitude.
- Best model chosen by a two-sample KS test against the observed CDF.

McNeill 2019 (AJ 157, 164):
- Same projected-area model, with survey cadence, per-measurement uncertainties drawn from the observed error distribution, the NEO spin-pole distribution of Tardioli et al. (2017), and a two-sample chi-square test (fits within chi^2 <= 2 chi^2_min accepted). PS1 limits: error <= 0.02 mag and alpha <= 20 deg.
- Phase-amplitude correction, Eq. 1: $\frac{b}{a}\ge10^{\frac{-0.4\Delta m}{1+s\alpha}}$ with s = 0.015 mag/deg, plus a polynomial fit to Zappala et al. 1990 Fig. 1 at larger alpha.

McNeill 2021 (ATLAS Trojans):
- All magnitudes are cast to absolute Hc and Ho with fitted H-G.
- The distribution of individual detections is compared with synthetic ATLAS-cadence populations (uniform error +/-0.05 mag) by KS, Mann-Whitney and chi-square tests.
- Selection: >= 100 o-band and >= 20 c-band observations, minimum alpha <= 5 deg, alpha coverage >= 6 deg.

'Extreme asteroids':
- Eq. 1: $A_{obs}=-2.5\log\frac{b}{a}-1.25\log\frac{a^2\cos^2\theta+c^2\sin^2\theta}{b^2\cos^2\theta+c^2\sin^2\theta}$, with theta called the latitude of the spin pole. At theta = 90 deg (spin perpendicular to the orbital plane) it reduces to Eq. 2: $A_{obs}=-2.5\log\frac{b}{a}$.
- Zappala relation, Eq. 24: $A(\alpha=0^\circ)=\frac{A_{obs}}{1+s\alpha}$ with s = 0.015 mag/deg.
methods.assumptions:
- Ellipsoids with geometric projection (no limb or scattering effects).
- Assumed spin-rate and pole distributions.
- Noise handled by forward simulation (uniform or empirical error distribution) rather than subtraction.
- Amplitude-phase relation linear for alpha < 40 deg.
methods.validation_reported:
VERIFIED.

McNeill 2016:
- Best fit 1 : 0.85 +/- 0.13 : 0.71 +/- 0.13 (Kryszczynska-based b/c distribution), within 1 sigma of the light-curve-based 1 : 0.76 +/- 0.13 : 0.62 +/- 0.11 (Kryszczynska et al. 2007).
- Robustness tests showed no differences: first vs last pair in a tracklet; alpha < 2 vs 8-10 deg; |ecliptic latitude| < 20 vs > 40 deg; first vs last 200 days.
- Cibulkova 2018 found no size trend using all measurements and suggested McNeill's 0.02-mag error cut as the reason.

McNeill 2019:
- Spitzer NEOs b/a = 0.72 +/- 0.08, PS1 NEOs 0.70 +/- 0.10, PS1 NEOs of 1-5 km 0.70 +/- 0.12.
- The model 'correctly reproduces the best fit' for synthetic samples with n > 300.
- It cites Erasmus et al. 2018 (KMTNet, about 1000 MBA partial light curves) giving b/a = 0.74 +/- 0.07.

Mommert et al. 2018 report the updated McNeill PS1 value 1 : 0.83 +/- 0.07 : 0.70 +/- 0.06, obtained with a better phase-angle amplitude correction.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
Population tools, not per-object amplitude estimators. Nortunen et al. (2017, App. B) show the consecutive-detection slope observable is degenerate with the rotation period.

What transfers to our problem:
- (a) Forward-simulating noise from the empirical error distribution, the right way to handle heterogeneous or missing errors.
- (b) Routine use of the Zappala correction $A(0)=A_{obs}/(1+s\alpha)$ when comparing amplitudes taken at different phase angles (our data span alpha of about 3-35 deg).

McNeill 2021 also notes that comparing sets of rotational amplitudes, rather than individual detections, requires contiguous observations.
methods.implementation_sketch:
Use as a simulation framework:
1. Inject ellipsoid light curves with realistic pole distributions, phase-angle amplitude scaling and our actual cadence, apparition structure and survey noise (including 0.1-mag rounding and surveys without errors) into the full pipeline.
2. Measure how the folded amplitude, the per-apparition eta or likelihood amplitudes, and their maxima relate to the input equator-on amplitude and to a simulated 'LCDB-like' single-apparition dense amplitude.
3. This directly quantifies the 25% deficit and the bias of any proposed estimator.

methods.name: Aspect-angle and phase-angle dependence of the observed amplitude: relating aspect-averaged or random-aspect amplitudes to elongation (Lacerda & Luu 2003; Masiero et al. 2009; Showalter et al. 2021; Zappala amplitude-phase relation as quoted therein)
methods.data_type: Analytic relations and statistical distributions, for ensembles and for single objects observed at many aspects.

papers.citation: Lacerda P., Luu J. 2003, Icarus 161, 174, 'On the detectability of lightcurves of Kuiper belt objects'
Masiero J., Jedicke R., Durech J., Gwyn S., Denneau L., Larsen J. 2009, Icarus 204, 145, 'The Thousand Asteroid Light Curve Survey' (DOI 10.1016/j.icarus.2009.06.012)

Showalter M. R., Benecchi S. D., Buie M. W., et al. 2021, Icarus 356, 114098, 'A Statistical Review of Light Curves and the Prevalence of Contact Binaries in the Kuiper Belt' (DOI 10.1016/j.icarus.2020.114098)

methods.algorithm:
VERIFIED.

Lacerda & Luu 2003 (axes normalized by b: $\bar a=a/b$, $\bar c=c/b$; theta the aspect angle):
- Eq. 2: $\Delta m=2.5\log\left(\frac{\bar a^2\cos^2\theta+\bar a^2\bar c^2\sin^2\theta}{\bar a^2\cos^2\theta+\bar c^2\sin^2\theta}\right)^{1/2}$
- At theta = pi/2, Eq. 3: $\Delta m=2.5\log\bar a$.
- Isotropic poles, Eq. 6a: $p_{\bar a,\bar c}(\mathrm{non\text{-}detection})=\frac{2\times\Omega(\theta_{min})}{4\pi}=1-\cos\theta_{min}$
- Eq. 7: $\cos\theta_{min}=\Psi(\bar a,\bar c)=\sqrt{\frac{\bar c^2(\bar a^2-K)}{\bar c^2(\bar a^2-K)+\bar a^2(K-1)}}$, with $K=10^{0.8\Delta m_{min}}$.
- Amplitude-phase relation quoted there: $A(\theta,0)=A(\theta,\alpha)/(1+m\alpha)$, with mean m(S) = 0.030, m(C) = 0.015 and m(M) = 0.013, citing Michalowski 1993. McNeill et al. use s = 0.015 mag/deg; Mommert et al. used 0.02 mag/deg.

Masiero 2009 (b = c, principal-axis rotation; theta the angle of the spin vector to the line of sight):
- Light curve: $m=2.5\log_{10}\sqrt{1+\left[\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^2-1\right]\cos^2(2\pi\phi)\sin^2\theta}$
- Eq. 1: $\Delta m=2.5\log\left[\cos^2\theta+\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^2\sin^2\theta\right]^{-1/2}$, used with isotropic poles to convert a debiased amplitude distribution into f(b/a).

Showalter 2021 (phi is the pole angle relative to the line of sight; for identical bodies with monotonic $\Delta m(\phi')$, $\phi'=\min(\phi,180^\circ-\phi)$):
- Eq. 1: $M(x)\equiv\mathrm{Prob}[\Delta m\le x]=\mathrm{Prob}[\phi'\le f(x)]$
- Isotropic poles, Eqs. 2-3: $M(\Delta m)=1-\cos\phi'(\Delta m)$
- With the line of sight in the orbit plane, $\cos\phi=\sin i\sin(\eta-\zeta)$, and Eq. 4: $M(x)=\mathrm{Prob}[|\sin i||\cos u|\ge\cos(f(x))]$
- Eq. 5: $M(x)=\frac{2}{\pi}\cos^{-1}(\cos(f(x))/|\sin i|)$
- Eq. 6a: $M(\Delta m)=0$ for $\phi'(\Delta m)<90^\circ-i$; Eq. 6b: $M=\frac{2}{\pi}\cos^{-1}(\cos\phi'(\Delta m)/|\sin i|)$ otherwise.
- For i = 90 deg, Eq. 7: $M(\Delta m)=\frac{2}{\pi}\phi'(\Delta m)$.
- For an obliquity PDF h(i), M is the h-weighted sum of Eq. 6.
methods.assumptions:
- Ellipsoidal (or modelled) shapes.
- Geometric scattering at small phase angle, or the Zappala linear correction for alpha <~ 40 deg.
- Poles isotropic or with a specified obliquity distribution.
- Observer in or near the orbital or ecliptic plane (Showalter; Nortunen App. A). For inclined orbits this is only approximate.
methods.validation_reported:
Analytic and statistical relations, not amplitude estimators; no LCDB validation numbers.
- Masiero 2009: the debiased CFHT amplitude distribution (amplitudes > 0.2 mag) is best fitted by f(b/a) proportional to (b/a)^2. A step-function fit is better for amplitudes > 0.1 mag and suggests about 75% round objects (b/a ~ 0.8) plus a distinct elongated group at b/a ~ 0.3.
- Showalter et al.: shape irregularities and albedo patterns each increase Delta m by 0.03 +/- 0.03 mag in their models (occasionally up to 0.1 mag).
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
These relations quantify the physical origin of our deficit and how to undo it.

For one object observed over many apparitions near the ecliptic, the aspect follows $\cos\theta\approx\sin\beta\cos\Lambda$ (Nortunen App. A; Showalter's $\cos\phi=\sin i\sin(\eta-\zeta)$). Such an object is therefore seen close to equator-on at some ecliptic longitudes, where the amplitude approaches $2.5\log(a/b)$ (Lacerda Eq. 3; Masiero Eq. 1). This is exact only for a zero-inclination orbit and observer. A fold of all apparitions, by contrast, averages over the aspect.

LCDB amplitudes are per-light-curve peak-to-peak values and are not phase-corrected (LCDB readme; McNeill et al. 2018, Fig. 24 caption), and AmpMax is the largest reported value with U >= 2-. Two literature-consistent comparisons follow:
- (a) per-apparition amplitudes, phase-matched or Zappala-corrected, against LCDB detail lines from the same apparition;
- (b) the maximum over apparitions, or the equator-on value from an aspect fit, against LCDB AmpMax.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1. For each apparition, compute the mean ecliptic longitude of the asteroid as seen from Earth (or the mean Earth-direction vector) and the mean phase angle.
2. Fit the per-apparition amplitudes $A_k$ (from the eta or likelihood methods) with $\Delta m_k=(1+s\bar\alpha_k)\,2.5\log[\cos^2\theta_k+p^2\sin^2\theta_k]^{-1/2}$, $\cos\theta_k=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{e}_k$, with free pole and p and s from taxonomy (0.013-0.03). This combines Masiero Eq. 1 with the Zappala relation; the combination is ours.
3. Report the equator-on amplitude $2.5\log(1/p)$ at alpha = 0, and the predicted amplitude at the geometry and phase angle of each LCDB entry.
4. Sanity check of the deficit (our derivation from Masiero Eq. 1). In the small-amplitude limit $\Delta m(\theta)\approx\Delta m_{eq}\sin^2\theta$. With $\cos\theta=\sin\beta\cos\Lambda$ (beta the spin co-latitude) and Lambda uniform, $\langle\Delta m\rangle/\Delta m_{eq}\approx1-\frac{1}{2}\sin^2\beta$. That is 0.5 for poles in the ecliptic, 1 for poles at the ecliptic poles and 2/3 for isotropic poles, the same order as our 25% deficit. A fold of combined data is not exactly the mean of per-apparition amplitudes, so treat this as order-of-magnitude only.

verified.other_relevant_facts:
LCDB definitions (verified in the LCDB readme, revised 2023 October 1, minorplanet.info/docs/lcdb_readme.pdf):
- 'All lightcurve amplitudes are peak-to-peak, not average-to-peak.'
- Summary AmpMin and AmpMax are the minimum and maximum reported amplitudes, using only detail lines with U >= 2-.
- Multiple detail lines for one reference are kept deliberately 'to allow statistical studies of lightcurve amplitude versus phase versus class (albedo)' (Sect. 4.1.1).
- LCDB amplitudes are not corrected for phase angle (stated in the Fig. 24 caption of McNeill et al. 2018, AJ 156, 282).
- So a multi-apparition average compared with AmpMax is biased low by construction.

Amplitude-phase relation, as quoted in papers actually read:
- Form: A(theta,0) = A(theta,alpha)/(1+m alpha) (Zappala et al. 1990, A&A 231, 548; not read directly).
- Lacerda & Luu 2003 give m(S) = 0.030, m(C) = 0.015, m(M) = 0.013, citing Michalowski 1993.
- McNeill et al. 2018 and 2019 use s = 0.015 mag/deg and state the relation is linear for alpha <= 40 deg.
- Lu & Jewitt 2019 (arXiv:1910.04923, AJ, DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/ab4ce4; full text read) quote Zappala as linear for alpha <= 50 deg. Their biaxial-ellipsoid models (Hapke-derived Kaasalainen scattering for C, S and V types; a/b of 2-7 only; equatorial viewing, so upper limits) give Delta m roughly proportional to alpha for alpha >~ 20 deg, slightly non-linear at alpha <~ 20 deg because of the opposition effect, and only weakly dependent on spectral type.
- Mommert et al. 2018 estimated a +40% amplitude overestimate at alpha = 19 deg with 0.02 mag/deg, but found it insignificant for their ensemble.
- With our alpha range of about 3-35 deg, this effect is of the same order as the 25% deficit and must be matched or corrected before comparing with LCDB.

Our own derivations (not from the papers):
(1) Rms-to-amplitude conversion.
- Small amplitudes: Nortunen's biaxial eta-A relation (Eq. 8) reduces to A_mag ~ 1.535 eta, and eta ~ 1.842 sigma_m. Hence A_mag ~ 2.83 sigma_m = 2*sqrt(2)*sigma_m, the sinusoid rule.
- Large amplitudes: use the exact Eq. 8.
- Mommert's empirical 1.51 x (2 sigma) = 3.02 sigma is close to 2*sqrt(2)*sigma. This suggests a noise-corrected 2*sqrt(2)*sigma per apparition is nearly unbiased against LCDB for A > 0.25 mag.
- Caveat: Mommert's Sect. 3.2 wording equates the amplitude with the weighted sigma, while the Fig. 1 caption, Table 1 and the Eurynome example indicate amplitude = 2 sigma.
(2) Noise and rounding.
- Rounding to 0.1 mag adds a quantization variance of 0.1^2/12 (sigma = 0.029 mag).
- This and the reported or estimated errors must be subtracted in quadrature. In Cibulkova's Eq. 12 this enters as 4 sigma_L^2 in intensity-squared units, with sigma_L ~ 0.921 sigma_m.
- Underestimated noise gives amplitudes that are too large and shapes that are too elongated. Cibulkova 2016 (Sect. 4.1), Cibulkova 2018 (Sect. 5.2) and Mommert 2018 (Sect. 5.1) all point to this for the Lowell (MPC) data.
(3) Compute the dispersion per apparition.
- A dispersion over the whole multi-year dataset also contains the aspect-dependent change of mean brightness between apparitions (Cibulkova Eqs. 6, 10), which is not rotational.
- Multi-apparition phase-curve fits handle this with a separate H_i per apparition:
  - Colazo et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.05412, Icarus): Eq. 1 is a sum over apparitions with common G1, G2 and per-apparition H_i, following Oszkiewicz et al. 2021. They did not correct for light-curve amplitude or geometry.
  - Robinson et al. 2024 (arXiv:2404.04657, MNRAS 531, 304; methods read): non-primary apparitions are fitted for H only with fixed slopes. They define F_app = sigma(H)/median[sigma(m_obs - m_fit)] (Eq. 8), the spread of H across apparitions over the median within-apparition residual scatter, with significant apparition effects for F_app >= 0.9. About 9000 asteroids show large H shifts between apparitions, interpreted as elongated shapes with obliquity near 90 deg. This is direct evidence that between-apparition variance is large and aspect-driven.
(4) Taking the maximum of noisy per-apparition estimates is biased upward. Use posterior or bootstrap distributions of the maximum, or an aspect-model fit.

Other verified facts:
- Number of points per estimate: Nortunen et al. 2017 find the eta error drops from about 50% with two points to close to 10% with five or six points (analytic estimate for a boxcar-like signal).
- Population sizes for CDF inversion: Nortunen used 1000 objects, LEADER requires N >~ 1000, and Cibulkova 2018 find b/a stable from about 800 objects with no beta information below 500. The earlier claim that '500 objects suffice' was not found in these papers and has been removed.
- Slow rotators: Cibulkova 2018 show that the eta method underestimates elongation (b/a drifts to about 1) for P > 12 h with PS1, because most PS1 data for an object come from a single night. Per-apparition windows avoid this for most periods.
- Sinusoid-based random-phase likelihoods are biased low for two-peaked or non-sinusoidal light curves:
  - Schemel & Brown: K2 Trojan means are about 50% larger than theirs, i.e. ZTF about 2/3 of K2. CORRECTED from '50% smaller'. A 0.25/0.1-mag two-peak test returned 0.1.
  - Bernardinelli et al.: 0.44 vs 0.85 mag for 2003 SQ317.
- Current practice: Erasmus et al. 2026 (arXiv:2609.07404; Sect. 3.5 read) measure amplitudes as max-min of a running average (window 10% of a cycle, wrapping in phase) of the folded, combined multi-year ATLAS light curve. methods.name: 1. Empirical amplitude-phase relation (APR): reduce amplitudes to zero phase angle (Zappala et al. 1990, as reproduced by later papers), with theoretical revisions (Gutierrez et al. 2006; Lu & Jewitt 2019)
methods.data_type: Peak-to-peak amplitudes from dense single-epoch light curves at a known phase angle alpha. It can also be applied to per-apparition amplitudes from sparse data, or to a combined fold at an effective (mean) phase angle.

methods.algorithm:
(a) Linear APR. Carbognani et al. 2017, eq. (2):
  A(\alpha) = A(0^\circ)\,(1 + m\alpha)
In their words, A is 'the amplitude (in mag) at the phase angle alpha (in deg), while m is a constant with dimension 1/deg that depends on the taxonomic type, i.e. m = 0.030 for S-type, m = 0.015 for C-type and m = 0.013 for M-type' [Zappala et al. 1990].

(b) Reduction to zero phase.
Polishook & Brosch 2009, eq. (2):
  A(0^0) = A(\alpha) / (1 + m\cdot\alpha)
They used 'the average value of m=0.023 deg-1 found by Zappala et al. (1990) from 27 different measurements', followed by A(0^0) = 2.5\cdot\log(a/b)_{min}.
Thirouin et al. 2016, eq. (6):
  \Delta m(\alpha = 0^\circ) = \frac{\Delta m(\alpha)}{1 + s\alpha}
Their eq. (7), 'assuming a viewing angle of 90 deg, an obliquity of 0 deg, and a phase angle alpha':
  \frac{a}{b} \ge 10^{0.4\Delta m(\alpha)/(1+s\alpha)}
The text says 'Combining Equations 4 and 5'; it is actually their eqs. (5) and (6). They quote s = 0.013 (M), 0.015 (C) and 0.030 (S) 'mag deg-1', from Zappala et al.'s analysis of 'lightcurves of more than 30 asteroids', and adopt s = 0.03.
McNeill et al. 2019, eq. (1), as printed:
  \frac{b}{a} \ge 10^{\frac{-0.4\Delta m}{1+s\alpha}}
The inequality direction is as printed; a lower limit on elongation would need b/a <=. They use s = 0.015 mag deg^-1 ('conservative') and state that the APR is linear for alpha < 40 deg. At larger alpha (Spitzer data) they use 'the non-linear relationship from Figure 1 of Zappala et al. (1990) as approximated with a polynomial fit'.
Navarro-Meza et al. 2021: \Delta m(0^\circ) = \Delta m(\alpha)/(1 + s\alpha), with s = 0.019 ('an average value'). 'Main belt asteroids are observed at alpha < 30 deg, so the correction factor is between 1 and 1.57'. They apply an average factor of 1.2 to LCDB maximum amplitudes (U = 3, 3-, 2+).
Lu & Jewitt 2019 state that Zappala et al. found the amplitude 'linearly proportional to phase angle for alpha <= 50 deg'.
Units: in the multiplicative form, m (or s) is per degree. Thirouin and McNeill label s as 'mag deg-1' while using the same multiplicative formula. The additive form A(0) + s*alpha was not seen in any paper I read.

(c) Gutierrez et al. 2006 (abstract-level, from search snippets only; full text not read):
- Mineralogy, regolith properties and small-scale roughness have a negligible effect on the APR.
- Large-scale topography adds a dispersion in the APR slope of about 0.010 mag deg^-1.
- Obliquity causes about 0.020 mag deg^-1 of slope dispersion: 'the larger the obliquity, the smaller the slope'.
- At intermediate aspect angles, a large obliquity can make the amplitude decrease with phase angle.
- A snippet of the A&A PDF also says obliquity has a negligible effect on the amplitude for alpha < 30 deg and becomes dominant at larger alpha. NOT verified in the full text.
Thirouin et al. 2016 summarize Gutierrez as giving 'an upper limit of 0.03 mag deg-1'.

(d) Model basis (Lu & Jewitt 2019).
- Disk-integrated brightness, eq. (1): L = \iint_{C_+} S(\alpha,\mu,\mu_0)\,d\sigma
- Kaasalainen phase function, eq. (3): f(\alpha) = A_0\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha}{D}\right) + K\alpha + 1
- Scattering law, eq. (4): S_{MK}(\alpha,\mu,\mu_0) = f(\alpha)\left(\frac{\mu\mu_0}{\mu+\mu_0} + C\mu\mu_0\right)
- For non-normalized fits, eq. (8) uses f(\alpha) = A_0\exp(-\alpha/D) + K\alpha + B.
- Amplitude, eq. (9): \Delta m = 2.5\log\left(\frac{L_{max}}{L_{min}}\right)
The models are biaxial ellipsoids (a > b = c) rotating about c, with viewing and illumination in the equatorial plane, so they give an 'upper limit to the amplitudes'. Axis ratios run from a/b = 2 to 7. C is fitted to Hapke models: 0.08-0.11 (C-type), 0.11-0.15 (S-type), 0.28-0.34 (V-type).
methods.assumptions:
- The amplitude grows linearly with alpha (stated as valid below about 40 deg by McNeill 2019, and up to 50 deg by Lu & Jewitt quoting Zappala).
- A single slope per taxonomic class, or a population average.
- Aspect and obliquity are ignored, although Gutierrez et al. identify obliquity as the main source of slope dispersion.
- Lu & Jewitt's models assume an equatorial geometry (an upper limit) and cover only a/b >= 2, which is more elongated than typical main-belt asteroids.
methods.validation_reported:
- Zappala 1990, via secondary sources: slopes from light curves of 'more than 30 asteroids' of S, M and C types (Thirouin), or an average m = 0.023 deg^-1 from 27 measurements (Polishook & Brosch). Not checked against the original.
- Carbognani et al. 2017: least-squares fit of eq. (2) to the dense light curves of 2011 UW158 (campaign of 31 nights, 2015 June 17 to Sept 26, spanning the 2015 July 19 Earth flyby). Post-flyby subset: A(0) = 0.49 ± 0.05 mag, A(0)m = 0.0203 ± 0.0009 mag/deg, m = 0.041 ± 0.005 deg^-1 ('compatible with an S-type'). Pre-flyby: A(0) = 0.016 ± 0.096 mag, A(0)m = 0.008 ± 0.001 mag/deg, m = 0.5 ± 3 deg^-1, i.e. unconstrained because the phase-angle range was narrower.
- Thirouin et al. 2016 (s = 0.03): the mean MANOS a/b fell from 1.54 to 1.23; for 2015 SO2, a/b went from 4.6 to 1.7 at alpha of about 60 deg.
- Lu & Jewitt 2019 models: 'For small values of a/b ... Delta m proportional to alpha for alpha >~ 20 deg, broadly confirming the result of Zappala'. Slightly non-linear for alpha <~ 20 deg because of the opposition effect. Only weakly dependent on spectral type; the amplitude increases slightly with albedo.
- Counter-evidence, Mommert et al. 2018: with 'an assumed average phase slope parameter of 0.02 mag/degree' and mean alpha = 19 deg, the APR predicts Gaia DR2 amplitudes about 40% too high. They found amplitudes lower than LCDB values instead, and conclude 'the effect of the solar phase angle on the lightcurve amplitude is insignificant for our ensemble analysis'.
- Related, Nortunen et al. 2017 (arXiv:1703.07178): in synthetic tests of their population (eta) method, 'the error caused by a non-zero phase angle is so small compared to other error sources that its effect is negligible' for alpha <= 30 deg. This concerns their error budget, not per-object amplitudes.
methods.applicability_to_our_data: Applicable, but by itself it cannot remove a deficit caused by geometry averaging. My reasoning (not from a paper): your phase-curve removal subtracts an additive HG1G2 term in magnitudes, which leaves the multiplicative amplitude scaling in place. The fold therefore has roughly A(0)(1 + m*alpha-bar), where alpha-bar is the data-weighted mean phase angle (your alpha spans about 3-35 deg). If LCDB detail lines were taken at a similar mean alpha, the APR scales both by about the same factor and does not explain a 25% deficit. The statement that LCDB dense light curves are 'typically at alpha 5-25 deg' is an assumption that I could not verify; check it against the phase-angle values stored on each LCDB detail line (the README says detail lines are split so amplitudes can be tied to PAB/phase values). Waszczak et al. 2015 note that LCDB light curves 'are often sampled over the shortest time window necessary to measure the period, and therefore generally do not require large or uncertain corrections due to phase angle effects'. Use the APR to put both your amplitudes and matched LCDB detail lines on alpha = 0 before comparing. The slope dispersion of about 0.01-0.02 per degree (Gutierrez) gives ±20-40% uncertainty in the correction factor at alpha = 20 deg, so a per-object slope fitted to your own data (Method 4) is better than the taxonomic table. Mommert 2018's null result shows the APR is not the dominant term in survey-versus-LCDB comparisons.
methods.implementation_sketch:
1) For each object, compute the effective phase angle of the fold, alpha_w = sum(w_i alpha_i)/sum(w_i), using the same weights as the Fourier fit.
2) Compute A_0 = A_fold/(1 + m*alpha_w), with m from taxonomy (S 0.030, C 0.015, M 0.013; 0.019-0.023 if unknown).
3) For every LCDB detail line with a phase angle, compute A_0,LCDB = A_LCDB/(1 + m*alpha_LCDB). Compare medians of A_0/A_0,LCDB.
4) Better: fit m per object with y_i = c_0 + (1 + m alpha_i) S(phi_i), where S is a 4-harmonic series. Solve by alternating linear least squares for (c_0, S) at fixed m with a 1-D search over m in [0, 0.06]. Report A_0 = ptp(S) and m with uncertainties. (This joint model is my suggestion; no paper uses it.)

methods.name: 2. Triaxial-ellipsoid amplitude-aspect relation (geometric scattering, zero phase), and amplitude-aspect fitting over many apparitions

methods.assumptions:
- Geometric scattering: brightness proportional to projected (illuminated) area.
- Opposition, or amplitudes first reduced to alpha = 0.
- Uniform albedo, principal-axis rotation about the shortest axis, and a smooth ellipsoid, so only the second harmonic is described.
- LEADER also assumes observers near the ecliptic, population-level inference, and N >~ 1000 objects.
methods.validation_reported:
- Thirouin 2016, McNeill 2016 and Nortunen 2017 treat the relation as standard geometry; no per-object validation.
- LEADER: the relative misfit ||C - Mw||/||C|| 'is usually less than 1% when the population contains at least 1000-2000 objects'. Synthetic tests show the recovered p is shifted toward elongated values; this is corrected by a shift Delta P (0.1 for WISE). beta is less accurate and tends to move away from the end points.
methods.applicability_to_our_data:
This geometry is part of the deficit, but the literature-comparable target must be chosen with care.

My own Monte Carlo (not from the literature) used eq. (a) with isotropic poles, an ecliptic observer, a/b = 1.2-1.8 and b/c = 1.0-1.2. The longitude-averaged amplitude is 0.54-0.64 of the equatorial value 2.5 log(a/b), which confirms the original summary's 0.53-0.63. Two points the original missed:
(i) For an ecliptic observer every pole gets an equatorial view at some longitude, so the per-object maximum equals 2.5 log(a/b).
(ii) The longitude-average is the expected amplitude of one light curve at a random epoch. A coherent average of per-apparition amplitudes therefore has no bias against an individual LCDB detail line taken at a random epoch.

A deficit against the LCDB appears only in three cases:
(1) The comparison is against AmpMax (the maximum over several lines) or against epochs that observers favoured.
(2) The folded amplitude falls below the mean of the per-apparition amplitudes, because extrema phases and light-curve shape change between apparitions (see other facts).
(3) Selection effects in published dense light curves.

To obtain literature-comparable values, do one of the following: compute A at each LCDB detail line's geometry; compare max_j A_j with AmpMax; or report the equatorial zero-phase amplitude 2.5 log(a/b). All three need a pole (Methods 3 and 5, or DAMIT).
methods.implementation_sketch:
1) Split the data into apparitions (Cibulkova et al. 2016 use gaps of at least 100 days).
2) Fit a 2-4 harmonic Fourier series per apparition, with P fixed and a free phase and amplitude (Method 4). Record A_j, the mean alpha_j and the mean asteroid-centric Earth direction e_j.
3) Reduce each amplitude: A_j0 = A_j/(1 + m alpha_j).
4) Grid over the pole (lambda, beta) with cos(xi_j) = v.e_j and v = [cos beta cos lambda, cos beta sin lambda, sin beta]^T. For each pole, fit a/b and b/c to A_j0 with eq. (a). Expect a lambda ± 180 deg ambiguity.
5) Output A_eq = 2.5 log10(a/b), and the predicted A at each LCDB detail-line epoch, eq. (a) times (1 + m alpha_LCDB). Bootstrap over apparitions.

methods.name: 3. Per-apparition normalized brightness dispersion and mean brightness versus aspect (Cibulkova et al. 2016): fitting a/b, b/c and the pole to multi-apparition sparse data. Population variant: LEADER applied to Pan-STARRS1 (Cibulkova et al. 2018)
